Introduction

Worldwide, railways are experiencing a continuously increasing travel demand. The existing railway networks have limited capacity and fewer and fewer extension possibilities due to the costly and land-consuming infrastructure. Especially at capacity bottlenecks such as in and around stations, extensions are often not available. To fulfil future railway demand in a different way, advanced signalling systems such as distance-to-go (DTG) systems are developed as capacityincreasing alternatives to conventional fixed-block multi-aspect signalling with automatic train protection systems.

In conventional fixed-block systems, the track is partitioned into blocks of fixed lengths which can be occupied by at most one train at a time.

The block entries are protected by trackside multi-aspect signals which indicate whether an approaching train can proceed, needs to start braking or is required to stop. The automatic train protection system supervises that the trains follow the signal aspects and intervenes when a train does not start braking after a brake indication. Hence, train separation distances are determined based on a number of blocks of fixed length.

Fixed-block DTG systems feature radio-based cab signalling and continuous braking curve supervision from the train front position to the block (or section) entry corresponding to the train’s end of movement authority (MA), i.e., the permission to move to a specific location under supervision. With this, brake indications no longer need to be provided at the entry of a block. Moreover, train separation distances become speed-dependent due to the approach distance to the first occupied block being based on the train’s absolute braking distance.

For effective railway operations, real-time traffic management is crucial. In case of small delays originating from variations in rolling stock, dwell times and driver behaviour, traffic management can apply rescheduling measures such as retiming, reordering and local rerouting to resolve track conflicts while minimising the delay propagation in the network. To support human dispatchers in taking mathematically optimised rescheduling decisions, conflict detection and resolution (CDR) models describing variants of the real-time railway traffic management or rescheduling problem are developed (Cacchiani et al., 2014; Pellegrini et al., 2014). In short, the problem can be formally described as follows: given a railway network and timetable together with delayed events, find a new timetable by rescheduling trains such that all track conflicts are resolved and total delay (or other relevant objective) is minimised.

The existing CDR models mostly refer to conventional fixed-block signalling systems. As a result, they are typically microscopic models that inherently rely on the discretisation of the track into fixed blocks. Moreover, they generally neglect changes in the speed profile to fit the adjusted timetable (Reynolds et al., 2022). Hence, these models cannot accurately capture the speed-dependent separation distances typical for DTG signalling due to the implementation of braking curve supervision (Versluis et al., 2024).

In this paper, we address the research gap regarding CDR for DTG signalling by developing a CDR model for DTG and applying it to assess the operational relevance of modelling CDR for DTG. To obtain a model that represents and identifies optimised rescheduling decisions for DTG railway operations, we propose enhancements for existing CDR models. The enhancements include the introduction of speed profile options and train blocking times considering train- and speed-dependent braking distances. These two enhancements are significant as they are crucial in enabling the modelling of train- and speed-dependent brake indication points in CDR models. As a proof of concept, we incorporate the enhancements into the state-of-the-art CDR model of RECIFE-MILP (Pellegrini et al., 2015), together with a distinction between switches and the rest of the track. The resulting model is assessed through a comparative analysis with the original one for conventional fixed-block signalling in two case studies, specifically in terms of total train delay and rescheduling decisions.

With this, the main contributions of the paper are:

A modelling approach for enhancing conflict detection and resolution models to apply to distance-to-go signalling, introducing train- and speed-dependent train separation and brake indication points.

A mixed-integer linear programming model for conflict detection and resolution under distance-to-go signalling, obtained by integrating distance-to-go principles into the state-of-the-art RECIFE-MILP model.

A comparative analysis illustrating the operational relevance of incorporating distance-to-go principles into conflict detection and resolution modelling, as different rescheduling decisions achieving reductions in total train delay are proposed.

The paper is organised as follows. In Section 2, the state-of-the-art related to the modelling of CDR for DTG signalling is provided.

Section 3 describes the enhancement approach for CDR models to describe DTG signalling.

The mathematical formulation of the fixed-block CDR model RECIFE-MILP enhanced for DTG signalling is presented in Section 4. Section 5 presents the results of the comparative analysis. Finally, Section 6 concludes the paper. State-of-the-art in conflict detection and resolution for distance-to-go signalling In this section, we provide an overview of the state-of-the-art relevant for the topic of modelling CDR under DTG signalling. Section 2.1 focuses on DTG signalling as the de-facto standard in the development of next-generation signalling systems. Section 2.2 provides an overview on modelling approaches for CDR existing in the literature.

2.1 Distance-to-go signalling systems In the development of next-generation signalling systems, DTG is the de-facto standard. For the mainline railways, DTG signalling is included within the European Train Control System (ETCS) and the Chinese Train Control System (CTCS). For metro lines, Communication-Based Train Control (CBTC) applies DTG signalling principles. Examples of deployed DTG systems are the fixed-block ETCS Level 2 with Trackside Train Detection (TTD) and the similar CTCS Level 3. The latter is designed for the Chinese high-speed (up to 300 km/h) railway lines (Xu et al., 2017). In this paper, we focus on ETCS Level 2 with TTD, hereafter referred to as ETCS L2, which is implemented on freight and passenger railways throughout the world (European Rail Supply Industry Association, 2022).

To enable cab signalling, ETCS L2 features radio communication between a radio block centre on the trackside and the trains as follows. The radio block centre receives train position information from a train. This information supports the request for a route extension to the interlocking system. Based on safety logic and input from TTD, the interlocking system sets and locks a new route for the train. As a next step, the radio block centre updates the MA before sending it to the train. With the received MA, the train recomputes and supervises a dynamic speed profile including continuous braking curves.

Corresponding to the braking curves, the brake indication point for a train can lie anywhere along the track. The end of authority, however, is consistently set at the end of a block or TTD section (TDS). The TDSs correspond to the parts of the track in which the presence of a train is automatically detected. Whether the end of authority corresponds to a block or TDS depends on the implemented ETCS L2 variant. It can also depend on whether it is on the open line, in a station or around switches. A schematic representation of the ETCS L2 system is provided in Figure 1. In the figure, two trains at the speed-dependent minimum separation distance are included.

Figure 1: Schematic layout of the minimum separation between two trains in a speed-distance diagram under ETCS L2 with (block) section boundaries, radio block centre (RBC) and radio communication (GSM-R). The separation is related to the brake indication point (IP) and the end of authority (EoA) depending on the braking curve.

Within ETCS and CTCS, more advanced application levels are being developed, but not yet deployed.

In particular, ETCS Level 2 with onboard train integrity monitoring (TIM), previously known as ETCS Level 3. This allows the end of authority to be located at the end of the last free virtual (non-physical) block, e.g., in ETCS Level 2 Virtual Block, or even at a safety margin behind the rear position of a moving train, e.g., in ETCS Level 2 Moving Block (European Railway Agency, 2016).

# CDR MILP for Railway Rescheduling under ETCS L2 (RECIFE-MILP style)
# Python implementation using PuLP

```python
import pulp

# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Input data (example instances; replace with real precomputed data)
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------

# Sets
T = ['T1', 'T2', 'T3']              # trains
R = ['r1', 'r2', 'r3_sw', 'r4']     # microscopic resources (track circuits / switches)
SWITCHES = ['r3_sw']                # resources that are switches
S = {                               # speed profile options per (train, resource)
    (i, r): [0, 1] for i in T for r in R
}

H = 3600.0                          # time horizon (s)
M = 2 * H                           # big-M

# Scheduled (unperturbed) passing times x_hat_{i,r}
sched = {
    ('T1', 'r1'): 0,   ('T1', 'r2'): 60,  ('T1', 'r3_sw'): 120, ('T1', 'r4'): 200,
    ('T2', 'r1'): 90,  ('T2', 'r2'): 160, ('T2', 'r3_sw'): 220, ('T2', 'r4'): 300,
    ('T3', 'r1'): 30,  ('T3', 'r2'): 100, ('T3', 'r3_sw'): 170, ('T3', 'r4'): 260,
}

# Weights w_i
w = {'T1': 1.0, 'T2': 1.0, 'T3': 1.0}

# Minimum running times per (train, resource, speed profile)  [seconds]
# (route through resource r ends at passing time at r; next resource is r+1)
min_rt = {
    (i, r, s): 50 + 10 * s          # placeholder: profile s=1 is slower
    for i in T for r in R[:-1] for s in S[(i, r)]
}

# Blocking (occupancy) times b_{i,r,s}: time resource r is blocked by train i
# arriving at passing time x_{i,r}, per speed profile (DTG braking distances)
blocking = {
    (i, r, s): 30 + 20 * s + 5 * r_idx      # placeholder tabulated values
    for i in T for (r, r_idx) in zip(R, range(len(R))) for s in S[(i, r)]
}

# Minimum headway between consecutive trains on same resource [seconds]
headway = {r: 25.0 for r in R}

# Recovery time for delay absorption [seconds]
recovery = 10.0

# Ordered chain of resources per train (route)
route = {i: R for i in T}

# Switch route conflict pairs: (switch, set of (train, route_id) in conflict)
# Trains using conflicting switch routes cannot occupy simultaneously ->
# handled by pairwise disjunction with extended blocking times on the switch.
switch_conflict_extra = {('r3_sw', i, j): 20.0 for i in T for j in T if i < j}

# Initial delays (from entry decisions / perturbed entry times)
initial_delay = {i: 0.0 for i in T}

# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Model
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------

model = pulp.LpProblem("CDR_ETCS_L2_Rescheduling", pulp.LpMinimize)

# ---- Variables ----
x = {(i, r): pulp.LpVariable(f"x_{i}_{r}", 0, H)
     for i in T for r in R}                       # passing times

delay = {i: pulp.LpVariable(f"delay_{i}", 0, H)
         for i in T}                              # terminal delay per train

y = {(i, r, s): pulp.LpVariable(f"y_{i}_{r}_{s}", cat="Binary")
     for i in T for r in R for s in S[(i, r)]}    # speed profile selection

z = {(i, j, r): pulp.LpVariable(f"z_{i}_{j}_{r}", cat="Binary")
     for i in T for j in T if i < j for r in R}   # ordering: 1 => i before j

# ---- Objective: minimize total weighted delay ----
model += pulp.lpSum(w[i] * delay[i] for i in T), "TotalWeightedDelay"

# ---- 1. Scheduled time constraints ----
for i in T:
    for r in route[i]:
        model += x[i, r] == sched[(i, r)] + delay[i], f"schedTime_{i}_{r}"

# ---- 2. Running time constraints with speed-profile big-M ----
for i in T:
    seq = route[i]
    for k in range(len(seq) - 1):
        r, r_next = seq[k], seq[k + 1]
        for s in S[(i, r)]:
            model += (x[i, r_next] - x[i, r]
                      >= min_rt[(i, r, s)] - M * (1 - y[i, r, s])),
                      f"runTime_{i}_{r}_{s}"
        model += pulp.lpSum(y[i, r, s] for s in S[(i, r)]) == 1, \
                 f"oneProfile_{i}_{r}"

# ---- 3. Resource occupancy / blocking-time disjunctions ----
for r in R:
    for idx, i in enumerate(T):
        for j in T[idx + 1:]:
            # If i before j: x_j >= x_i + b_i ; else x_i >= x_j + b_j
            b_i = pulp.lpSum(blocking[(i, r, s)] * y[i, r, s]
                             for s in S[(i, r)])
            b_j = pulp.lpSum(blocking[(j, r, s)] * y[j, r, s]
                             for s in S[(j, r)])
            # z = 1 -> i before j: x_j >= x_i + b_i - M(1-z)
            model += (x[j, r] - x[i, r] >= b_i - M * (1 - z[i, j, r])),
                      f"block_{i}_{j}_{r}_a"
            # z = 0 -> j before i: x_i >= x_j + b_j - M*z
            model += (x[i, r] - x[j, r] >= b_j - M * z[i, j, r]),
                      f"block_{i}_{j}_{r}_b"

# ---- 4. Switch route conflict constraints (extra separation) ----
for r in SWITCHES:
    for i in T:
        for j in T:
            if i < j:
                extra = switch_conflict_extra[(r, i, j)]
                b_i = pulp.lpSum(blocking[(i, r, s)] * y[i, r, s]
                                 for s in S[(i, r)]) + extra
                b_j = pulp.lpSum(blocking[(j, r, s)] * y[j, r, s]
                                 for s in S[(j, r)]) + extra
                model += (x[j, r] - x[i, r] >= b_i - M * (1 - z[i, j, r])),
                          f"swConf_{i}_{j}_{r}_a"
                model += (x[i, r] - x[j, r] >= b_j - M * z[i, j, r]),
                          f"swConf_{i}_{j}_{r}_b"

# ---- 5. Headway constraints between consecutive trains on same resource ----
for r in R:
    for idx, i in enumerate(T):
        for j in T[idx + 1:]:
            # enforced via strengthened disjunction: separation >= headway
            model += (x[j, r] - x[i, r]
                      >= headway[r] - M * (1 - z[i, j, r])),
                      f"headway_{i}_{j}_{r}_a"
            model += (x[i, r] - x[j, r]
                      >= headway[r] - M * z[i, j, r]),
                      f"headway_{i}_{j}_{r}_b"

# ---- 6. Delay propagation along the route ----
for i in T:
    seq = route[i]
    for k in range(len(seq) - 1):
        r, r_next = seq[k], seq[k + 1]
        model += ((x[i, r_next] - sched[(i, r_next)])
                  >= (x[i, r] - sched[(i, r)]) - recovery),
                  f"delayProp_{i}_{r}"

    # terminal delay definition
    model += delay[i] >= x[i, seq[-1]] - sched[(i, seq[-1])], \
             f"delayDef_{i}"

# ---- 7. Time horizon bounds ----
for i in T:
    for r in route[i]:
        model += x[i, r] <= H, f"horizon_{i}_{r}"

# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Solve
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------

solver = pulp.PULP_CBC_CMD(msg=True)
model.solve(solver)

print("Status:", pulp.LpStatus[model.status])
for i in T:
    print(f"Train {i}: terminal delay = {delay[i].value():.2f} s")
for i in T:
    print(f"Train {i} passing times:",
          {r: round(x[i, r].value(), 2) for r in route[i]})
```

**Notes on the formulation**

- **Blocking times** `b[i,r,s]` are tabulated offline per (train, resource, speed profile) following ETCS L2 DTG principles: they embed braking curves to the EoA at TTD/block boundaries, switch locking, and sighting times; the linear combination `Σ_s b·y` makes the disjunctive constraint profile-dependent.
- **Disjunctive pairwise ordering** uses standard big-M: binary `z[i,j,r]=1` means train `i` passes resource `r` before `j`, activating exactly one side of each disjunction.
- **Switch conflicts** reuse the same disjunctive pattern on switch resources with additional separation (route setting/release times).
- **Headways** are imposed as minimum separation of passing times on shared resources, consistent with the blocking-time logic.
- Replace the placeholder tables (`sched`, `min_rt`, `blocking`) with the actual precomputed offline data for a real instance.

                                 for s in S[(i, r)]) + extra

                                 for s in S[(j, r)]) + extra

                          f"swConf_{i}_{j}_{r}_a"
                model += (x[i, r] - x[j, r] >= b_j - M * z[i, j, r]),
                          f"swConf_{i}_{j}_{r}_b"

# ---- 5. Headway constraints between consecutive trains on same resource ----
for r in R:
    for idx, i in enumerate(T):
        for j in T[idx + 1:]:

            model += (x[j, r] - x[i, r]
                      >= headway[r] - M * (1 - z[i, j, r])),
                      f"headway_{i}_{j}_{r}_a"
            model += (x[i, r] - x[j, r]
                      >= headway[r] - M * z[i, j, r]),
                      f"headway_{i}_{j}_{r}_b"

for i in T:
    seq = route[i]
    for k in range(len(seq) - 1):
        r, r_next = seq[k], seq[k + 1]

                  >= (x[i, r] - sched[(i, r)]) - recovery),

             f"delayDef_{i}"

# Solve
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------

model.solve(solver)

for i in T:

Introduction

Worldwide, railways are experiencing a continuously increasing travel demand. The existing railway networks have limited capacity and fewer and fewer extension possibilities due to the costly and land-consuming infrastructure. Especially at capacity bottlenecks such as in and around stations, extensions are often not available. To fulfil future railway demand in a different way, advanced signalling systems such as distance-to-go (DTG) systems are developed as capacityincreasing alternatives to conventional fixed-block multi-aspect signalling with automatic train protection systems.

In conventional fixed-block systems, the track is partitioned into blocks of fixed lengths which can be occupied by at most one train at a time.

The block entries are protected by trackside multi-aspect signals which indicate whether an approaching train can proceed, needs to start braking or is required to stop. The automatic train protection system supervises that the trains follow the signal aspects and intervenes when a train does not start braking after a brake indication. Hence, train separation distances are determined based on a number of blocks of fixed length.

Fixed-block DTG systems feature radio-based cab signalling and continuous braking curve supervision from the train front position to the block (or section) entry corresponding to the train’s end of movement authority (MA), i.e., the permission to move to a specific location under supervision. With this, brake indications no longer need to be provided at the entry of a block. Moreover, train separation distances become speed-dependent due to the approach distance to the first occupied block being based on the train’s absolute braking distance.

For effective railway operations, real-time traffic management is crucial. In case of small delays originating from variations in rolling stock, dwell times and driver behaviour, traffic management can apply rescheduling measures such as retiming, reordering and local rerouting to resolve track conflicts while minimising the delay propagation in the network. To support human dispatchers in taking mathematically optimised rescheduling decisions, conflict detection and resolution (CDR) models describing variants of the real-time railway traffic management or rescheduling problem are developed (Cacchiani et al., 2014; Pellegrini et al., 2014). In short, the problem can be formally described as follows: given a railway network and timetable together with delayed events, find a new timetable by rescheduling trains such that all track conflicts are resolved and total delay (or other relevant objective) is minimised.

The existing CDR models mostly refer to conventional fixed-block signalling systems. As a result, they are typically microscopic models that inherently rely on the discretisation of the track into fixed blocks. Moreover, they generally neglect changes in the speed profile to fit the adjusted timetable (Reynolds et al., 2022). Hence, these models cannot accurately capture the speed-dependent separation distances typical for DTG signalling due to the implementation of braking curve supervision (Versluis et al., 2024).

In this paper, we address the research gap regarding CDR for DTG signalling by developing a CDR model for DTG and applying it to assess the operational relevance of modelling CDR for DTG. To obtain a model that represents and identifies optimised rescheduling decisions for DTG railway operations, we propose enhancements for existing CDR models. The enhancements include the introduction of speed profile options and train blocking times considering train- and speed-dependent braking distances. These two enhancements are significant as they are crucial in enabling the modelling of train- and speed-dependent brake indication points in CDR models. As a proof of concept, we incorporate the enhancements into the state-of-the-art CDR model of RECIFE-MILP (Pellegrini et al., 2015), together with a distinction between switches and the rest of the track. The resulting model is assessed through a comparative analysis with the original one for conventional fixed-block signalling in two case studies, specifically in terms of total train delay and rescheduling decisions.

With this, the main contributions of the paper are:

A modelling approach for enhancing conflict detection and resolution models to apply to distance-to-go signalling, introducing train- and speed-dependent train separation and brake indication points.

A mixed-integer linear programming model for conflict detection and resolution under distance-to-go signalling, obtained by integrating distance-to-go principles into the state-of-the-art RECIFE-MILP model.

A comparative analysis illustrating the operational relevance of incorporating distance-to-go principles into conflict detection and resolution modelling, as different rescheduling decisions achieving reductions in total train delay are proposed.

The paper is organised as follows. In Section 2, the state-of-the-art related to the modelling of CDR for DTG signalling is provided.

Section 3 describes the enhancement approach for CDR models to describe DTG signalling.

The mathematical formulation of the fixed-block CDR model RECIFE-MILP enhanced for DTG signalling is presented in Section 4. Section 5 presents the results of the comparative analysis. Finally, Section 6 concludes the paper. State-of-the-art in conflict detection and resolution for distance-to-go signalling In this section, we provide an overview of the state-of-the-art relevant for the topic of modelling CDR under DTG signalling. Section 2.1 focuses on DTG signalling as the de-facto standard in the development of next-generation signalling systems. Section 2.2 provides an overview on modelling approaches for CDR existing in the literature.

2.1 Distance-to-go signalling systems In the development of next-generation signalling systems, DTG is the de-facto standard. For the mainline railways, DTG signalling is included within the European Train Control System (ETCS) and the Chinese Train Control System (CTCS). For metro lines, Communication-Based Train Control (CBTC) applies DTG signalling principles. Examples of deployed DTG systems are the fixed-block ETCS Level 2 with Trackside Train Detection (TTD) and the similar CTCS Level 3. The latter is designed for the Chinese high-speed (up to 300 km/h) railway lines (Xu et al., 2017). In this paper, we focus on ETCS Level 2 with TTD, hereafter referred to as ETCS L2, which is implemented on freight and passenger railways throughout the world (European Rail Supply Industry Association, 2022).

To enable cab signalling, ETCS L2 features radio communication between a radio block centre on the trackside and the trains as follows. The radio block centre receives train position information from a train. This information supports the request for a route extension to the interlocking system. Based on safety logic and input from TTD, the interlocking system sets and locks a new route for the train. As a next step, the radio block centre updates the MA before sending it to the train. With the received MA, the train recomputes and supervises a dynamic speed profile including continuous braking curves.

Corresponding to the braking curves, the brake indication point for a train can lie anywhere along the track. The end of authority, however, is consistently set at the end of a block or TTD section (TDS). The TDSs correspond to the parts of the track in which the presence of a train is automatically detected. Whether the end of authority corresponds to a block or TDS depends on the implemented ETCS L2 variant. It can also depend on whether it is on the open line, in a station or around switches. A schematic representation of the ETCS L2 system is provided in Figure 1. In the figure, two trains at the speed-dependent minimum separation distance are included.

Figure 1: Schematic layout of the minimum separation between two trains in a speed-distance diagram under ETCS L2 with (block) section boundaries, radio block centre (RBC) and radio communication (GSM-R). The separation is related to the brake indication point (IP) and the end of authority (EoA) depending on the braking curve.

Within ETCS and CTCS, more advanced application levels are being developed, but not yet deployed.

In particular, ETCS Level 2 with onboard train integrity monitoring (TIM), previously known as ETCS Level 3. This allows the end of authority to be located at the end of the last free virtual (non-physical) block, e.g., in ETCS Level 2 Virtual Block, or even at a safety margin behind the rear position of a moving train, e.g., in ETCS Level 2 Moving Block (European Railway Agency, 2016).

# CDR MILP for Railway Rescheduling under ETCS L2 (RECIFE-MILP style)
# Python implementation using PuLP

```python
import pulp

# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Input data (example instances; replace with real precomputed data)
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------

# Sets
T = ['T1', 'T2', 'T3']              # trains
R = ['r1', 'r2', 'r3_sw', 'r4']     # microscopic resources (track circuits / switches)
SWITCHES = ['r3_sw']                # resources that are switches
S = {                               # speed profile options per (train, resource)
    (i, r): [0, 1] for i in T for r in R
}

H = 3600.0                          # time horizon (s)
M = 2 * H                           # big-M

# Scheduled (unperturbed) passing times x_hat_{i,r}
sched = {
    ('T1', 'r1'): 0,   ('T1', 'r2'): 60,  ('T1', 'r3_sw'): 120, ('T1', 'r4'): 200,
    ('T2', 'r1'): 90,  ('T2', 'r2'): 160, ('T2', 'r3_sw'): 220, ('T2', 'r4'): 300,
    ('T3', 'r1'): 30,  ('T3', 'r2'): 100, ('T3', 'r3_sw'): 170, ('T3', 'r4'): 260,
}

# Weights w_i
w = {'T1': 1.0, 'T2': 1.0, 'T3': 1.0}

# Minimum running times per (train, resource, speed profile)  [seconds]
# (route through resource r ends at passing time at r; next resource is r+1)
min_rt = {
    (i, r, s): 50 + 10 * s          # placeholder: profile s=1 is slower
    for i in T for r in R[:-1] for s in S[(i, r)]
}

# Blocking (occupancy) times b_{i,r,s}: time resource r is blocked by train i
# arriving at passing time x_{i,r}, per speed profile (DTG braking distances)
blocking = {
    (i, r, s): 30 + 20 * s + 5 * r_idx      # placeholder tabulated values
    for i in T for (r, r_idx) in zip(R, range(len(R))) for s in S[(i, r)]
}

# Minimum headway between consecutive trains on same resource [seconds]
headway = {r: 25.0 for r in R}

# Recovery time for delay absorption [seconds]
recovery = 10.0

# Ordered chain of resources per train (route)
route = {i: R for i in T}

# Switch route conflict pairs: (switch, set of (train, route_id) in conflict)
# Trains using conflicting switch routes cannot occupy simultaneously ->
# handled by pairwise disjunction with extended blocking times on the switch.
switch_conflict_extra = {('r3_sw', i, j): 20.0 for i in T for j in T if i < j}

# Initial delays (from entry decisions / perturbed entry times)
initial_delay = {i: 0.0 for i in T}

# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Model
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------

model = pulp.LpProblem("CDR_ETCS_L2_Rescheduling", pulp.LpMinimize)

# ---- Variables ----
x = {(i, r): pulp.LpVariable(f"x_{i}_{r}", 0, H)
     for i in T for r in R}                       # passing times

delay = {i: pulp.LpVariable(f"delay_{i}", 0, H)
         for i in T}                              # terminal delay per train

y = {(i, r, s): pulp.LpVariable(f"y_{i}_{r}_{s}", cat="Binary")
     for i in T for r in R for s in S[(i, r)]}    # speed profile selection

z = {(i, j, r): pulp.LpVariable(f"z_{i}_{j}_{r}", cat="Binary")
     for i in T for j in T if i < j for r in R}   # ordering: 1 => i before j

# ---- Objective: minimize total weighted delay ----
model += pulp.lpSum(w[i] * delay[i] for i in T), "TotalWeightedDelay"

# ---- 1. Scheduled time constraints ----
for i in T:
    for r in route[i]:
        model += x[i, r] == sched[(i, r)] + delay[i], f"schedTime_{i}_{r}"

# ---- 2. Running time constraints with speed-profile big-M ----
for i in T:
    seq = route[i]
    for k in range(len(seq) - 1):
        r, r_next = seq[k], seq[k + 1]
        for s in S[(i, r)]:
            model += (x[i, r_next] - x[i, r]
                      >= min_rt[(i, r, s)] - M * (1 - y[i, r, s])),
                      f"runTime_{i}_{r}_{s}"
        model += pulp.lpSum(y[i, r, s] for s in S[(i, r)]) == 1, \
                 f"oneProfile_{i}_{r}"

# ---- 3. Resource occupancy / blocking-time disjunctions ----
for r in R:
    for idx, i in enumerate(T):
        for j in T[idx + 1:]:
            # If i before j: x_j >= x_i + b_i ; else x_i >= x_j + b_j
            b_i = pulp.lpSum(blocking[(i, r, s)] * y[i, r, s]
                             for s in S[(i, r)])
            b_j = pulp.lpSum(blocking[(j, r, s)] * y[j, r, s]
                             for s in S[(j, r)])
            # z = 1 -> i before j: x_j >= x_i + b_i - M(1-z)
            model += (x[j, r] - x[i, r] >= b_i - M * (1 - z[i, j, r])),
                      f"block_{i}_{j}_{r}_a"
            # z = 0 -> j before i: x_i >= x_j + b_j - M*z
            model += (x[i, r] - x[j, r] >= b_j - M * z[i, j, r]),
                      f"block_{i}_{j}_{r}_b"

# ---- 4. Switch route conflict constraints (extra separation) ----
for r in SWITCHES:
    for i in T:
        for j in T:
            if i < j:
                extra = switch_conflict_extra[(r, i, j)]
                b_i = pulp.lpSum(blocking[(i, r, s)] * y[i, r, s]
                                 for s in S[(i, r)]) + extra
                b_j = pulp.lpSum(blocking[(j, r, s)] * y[j, r, s]
                                 for s in S[(j, r)]) + extra
                model += (x[j, r] - x[i, r] >= b_i - M * (1 - z[i, j, r])),
                          f"swConf_{i}_{j}_{r}_a"
                model += (x[i, r] - x[j, r] >= b_j - M * z[i, j, r]),
                          f"swConf_{i}_{j}_{r}_b"

# ---- 5. Headway constraints between consecutive trains on same resource ----
for r in R:
    for idx, i in enumerate(T):
        for j in T[idx + 1:]:
            # enforced via strengthened disjunction: separation >= headway
            model += (x[j, r] - x[i, r]
                      >= headway[r] - M * (1 - z[i, j, r])),
                      f"headway_{i}_{j}_{r}_a"
            model += (x[i, r] - x[j, r]
                      >= headway[r] - M * z[i, j, r]),
                      f"headway_{i}_{j}_{r}_b"

# ---- 6. Delay propagation along the route ----
for i in T:
    seq = route[i]
    for k in range(len(seq) - 1):
        r, r_next = seq[k], seq[k + 1]
        model += ((x[i, r_next] - sched[(i, r_next)])
                  >= (x[i, r] - sched[(i, r)]) - recovery),
                  f"delayProp_{i}_{r}"

    # terminal delay definition
    model += delay[i] >= x[i, seq[-1]] - sched[(i, seq[-1])], \
             f"delayDef_{i}"

# ---- 7. Time horizon bounds ----
for i in T:
    for r in route[i]:
        model += x[i, r] <= H, f"horizon_{i}_{r}"

# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Solve
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------

solver = pulp.PULP_CBC_CMD(msg=True)
model.solve(solver)

print("Status:", pulp.LpStatus[model.status])
for i in T:
    print(f"Train {i}: terminal delay = {delay[i].value():.2f} s")
for i in T:
    print(f"Train {i} passing times:",
          {r: round(x[i, r].value(), 2) for r in route[i]})
```

**Notes on the formulation**

- **Blocking times** `b[i,r,s]` are tabulated offline per (train, resource, speed profile) following ETCS L2 DTG principles: they embed braking curves to the EoA at TTD/block boundaries, switch locking, and sighting times; the linear combination `Σ_s b·y` makes the disjunctive constraint profile-dependent.
- **Disjunctive pairwise ordering** uses standard big-M: binary `z[i,j,r]=1` means train `i` passes resource `r` before `j`, activating exactly one side of each disjunction.
- **Switch conflicts** reuse the same disjunctive pattern on switch resources with additional separation (route setting/release times).
- **Headways** are imposed as minimum separation of passing times on shared resources, consistent with the blocking-time logic.
- Replace the placeholder tables (`sched`, `min_rt`, `blocking`) with the actual precomputed offline data for a real instance.

# CDR Model for Railway Rescheduling under ETCS L2 Distance-to-Go Signalling

## Assumptions
- Speed profiles are precomputed offline as discrete options per (train, resource); blocking times embed DTG braking curves to the end of authority (EoA) at TTD/block boundaries, and are tabulated per (train, resource, speed profile).
- Resources are microscopic: plain track circuits and switches (switches distinguished by extra route-locking separation).
- Delay is measured at the last resource of each train's route; big-M disjunctive formulations keep the model linear.

## Sets and Parameters
- $i, j \in T$: trains; $r \in R$: microscopic resources (track circuits, switches), $\mathit{SW} \subset R$ switches; $s \in S_{i,r}$: speed profile options.
- $\hat{x}_{i,r}$: scheduled passing time; $H$: time horizon; $M$: big-M.
- $\underline{rt}_{i,r,s}$: minimum running time under profile $s$.
- $b_{i,r,s}$: blocking (occupancy) time of train $i$ on resource $r$ under profile $s$ (speed- and train-dependent, per DTG braking distance).
- $h_r$: minimum headway on $r$; $\Delta_{i,r}^{rec}$: recovery time; $\delta_i$: initial delay; $w_i$: delay weight.

## Variables
- $x_{i,r} \ge 0$: actual passing time of train $i$ at resource $r$.
- $d_i \ge 0$: terminal delay of train $i$.
- $y_{i,r,s} \in \{0,1\}$: speed profile selection.
- $z_{i,j,r} \in \{0,1\}$ for $i<j$: ordering on $r$ ($1$ ⇒ $i$ before $j$).

## Objective
$$\min \; \sum_{i \in T} w_i \, d_i$$

## Constraints

**1. Scheduled times and initial delays**
$$x_{i,r} = \hat{x}_{i,r} + d_i \quad \forall i \in T,\; r \in \text{route}(i)$$
with $d_i \ge \delta_i$ (or scheduled time shifted by the perturbed entry time).

**2. Running times with speed-profile selection**
$$\sum_{s \in S_{i,r}} y_{i,r,s} = 1 \quad \forall i, r$$
$$x_{i,r'} - x_{i,r} \ge \underline{rt}_{i,r,s} - M(1 - y_{i,r,s}) \quad \forall i,\; (r,r') \text{ consecutive},\; s \in S_{i,r}$$

**3. Blocking-time disjunctions (DTG, speed-dependent separation)**
Let $B_{i,r} = \sum_{s} b_{i,r,s}\, y_{i,r,s}$. For each resource $r$ and pair $i<j$:
$$x_{j,r} - x_{i,r} \ge B_{i,r} - M(1 - z_{i,j,r})$$
$$x_{i,r} - x_{j,r} \ge B_{j,r} - M\, z_{i,j,r}$$
Exactly one ordering is active, ensuring no simultaneous occupancy of the blocked resource.

**4. Switch route-conflict constraints** — for $r \in \mathit{SW}$, same disjunction with enlarged blocking times $B_{i,r} + e_{r,ij}$ (route setting/locking/release separation for conflicting switch routes):
$$x_{j,r} - x_{i,r} \ge B_{i,r} + e_{r,ij} - M(1 - z_{i,j,r})$$
$$x_{i,r} - x_{j,r} \ge B_{j,r} + e_{r,ij} - M\, z_{i,j,r}$$

**5. Minimum headways** — for each resource $r$ and pair $i<j$:
$$x_{j,r} - x_{i,r} \ge h_r - M(1 - z_{i,j,r})$$
$$x_{i,r} - x_{j,r} \ge h_r - M\, z_{i,j,r}$$

**6. Delay propagation / recovery**
$$(x_{i,r'} - \hat{x}_{i,r'}) \ge (x_{i,r} - \hat{x}_{i,r}) - \Delta^{rec}_{i,r} \quad \forall i,\; \text{consecutive } (r,r')$$

**7. Terminal delay definition**
$$d_i \ge x_{i,r_{\text{last}}(i)} - \hat{x}_{i,r_{\text{last}}(i)} \quad \forall i \in T$$

**8. Horizon bounds**
$$0 \le x_{i,r} \le H \quad \forall i, r$$

The key DTG enhancement over conventional fixed-block RECIFE-MILP is constraint 3: blocking times $b_{i,r,s}$ depend on the train and its selected speed profile (speed-dependent braking distances to the EoA), linearized via the profile-selection binaries $y_{i,r,s}$.

## Constraints

**1. Scheduled times and initial delays**
$$x_{i,r} = \hat{x}_{i,r} + d_i \quad \forall i \in T,\; r \in \text{route}(i)$$
with $d_i \ge \delta_i$ (or scheduled time shifted by the perturbed entry time).

**2. Running times with speed-profile selection**
$$\sum_{s \in S_{i,r}} y_{i,r,s} = 1 \quad \forall i, r$$
$$x_{i,r'} - x_{i,r} \ge \underline{rt}_{i,r,s} - M(1 - y_{i,r,s}) \quad \forall i,\; (r,r') \text{ consecutive},\; s \in S_{i,r}$$

Let $B_{i,r} = \sum_{s} b_{i,r,s}\, y_{i,r,s}$. For each resource $r$ and pair $i<j$:
$$x_{j,r} - x_{i,r} \ge B_{i,r} - M(1 - z_{i,j,r})$$
$$x_{i,r} - x_{j,r} \ge B_{j,r} - M\, z_{i,j,r}$$
Exactly one ordering is active, ensuring no simultaneous occupancy of the blocked resource.

**4. Switch route-conflict constraints** — for $r \in \mathit{SW}$, same disjunction with enlarged blocking times $B_{i,r} + e_{r,ij}$ (route setting/locking/release separation for conflicting switch routes):
$$x_{j,r} - x_{i,r} \ge B_{i,r} + e_{r,ij} - M(1 - z_{i,j,r})$$
$$x_{i,r} - x_{j,r} \ge B_{j,r} + e_{r,ij} - M\, z_{i,j,r}$$

**5. Minimum headways** — for each resource $r$ and pair $i<j$:
$$x_{j,r} - x_{i,r} \ge h_r - M(1 - z_{i,j,r})$$
$$x_{i,r} - x_{j,r} \ge h_r - M\, z_{i,j,r}$$

**6. Delay propagation / recovery**
$$(x_{i,r'} - \hat{x}_{i,r'}) \ge (x_{i,r} - \hat{x}_{i,r}) - \Delta^{rec}_{i,r} \quad \forall i,\; \text{consecutive } (r,r')$$

**7. Terminal delay definition**
$$d_i \ge x_{i,r_{\text{last}}(i)} - \hat{x}_{i,r_{\text{last}}(i)} \quad \forall i \in T$$

$$0 \le x_{i,r} \le H \quad \forall i, r$$

Introduction

Worldwide, railways are experiencing a continuously increasing travel demand. The existing railway networks have limited capacity and fewer and fewer extension possibilities due to the costly and land-consuming infrastructure. Especially at capacity bottlenecks such as in and around stations, extensions are often not available. To fulfil future railway demand in a different way, advanced signalling systems such as distance-to-go (DTG) systems are developed as capacityincreasing alternatives to conventional fixed-block multi-aspect signalling with automatic train protection systems.

In conventional fixed-block systems, the track is partitioned into blocks of fixed lengths which can be occupied by at most one train at a time.

The block entries are protected by trackside multi-aspect signals which indicate whether an approaching train can proceed, needs to start braking or is required to stop. The automatic train protection system supervises that the trains follow the signal aspects and intervenes when a train does not start braking after a brake indication. Hence, train separation distances are determined based on a number of blocks of fixed length.

Fixed-block DTG systems feature radio-based cab signalling and continuous braking curve supervision from the train front position to the block (or section) entry corresponding to the train’s end of movement authority (MA), i.e., the permission to move to a specific location under supervision. With this, brake indications no longer need to be provided at the entry of a block. Moreover, train separation distances become speed-dependent due to the approach distance to the first occupied block being based on the train’s absolute braking distance.

For effective railway operations, real-time traffic management is crucial. In case of small delays originating from variations in rolling stock, dwell times and driver behaviour, traffic management can apply rescheduling measures such as retiming, reordering and local rerouting to resolve track conflicts while minimising the delay propagation in the network. To support human dispatchers in taking mathematically optimised rescheduling decisions, conflict detection and resolution (CDR) models describing variants of the real-time railway traffic management or rescheduling problem are developed (Cacchiani et al., 2014; Pellegrini et al., 2014). In short, the problem can be formally described as follows: given a railway network and timetable together with delayed events, find a new timetable by rescheduling trains such that all track conflicts are resolved and total delay (or other relevant objective) is minimised.

The existing CDR models mostly refer to conventional fixed-block signalling systems. As a result, they are typically microscopic models that inherently rely on the discretisation of the track into fixed blocks. Moreover, they generally neglect changes in the speed profile to fit the adjusted timetable (Reynolds et al., 2022). Hence, these models cannot accurately capture the speed-dependent separation distances typical for DTG signalling due to the implementation of braking curve supervision (Versluis et al., 2024).

In this paper, we address the research gap regarding CDR for DTG signalling by developing a CDR model for DTG and applying it to assess the operational relevance of modelling CDR for DTG. To obtain a model that represents and identifies optimised rescheduling decisions for DTG railway operations, we propose enhancements for existing CDR models. The enhancements include the introduction of speed profile options and train blocking times considering train- and speed-dependent braking distances. These two enhancements are significant as they are crucial in enabling the modelling of train- and speed-dependent brake indication points in CDR models. As a proof of concept, we incorporate the enhancements into the state-of-the-art CDR model of RECIFE-MILP (Pellegrini et al., 2015), together with a distinction between switches and the rest of the track. The resulting model is assessed through a comparative analysis with the original one for conventional fixed-block signalling in two case studies, specifically in terms of total train delay and rescheduling decisions.

With this, the main contributions of the paper are:

A modelling approach for enhancing conflict detection and resolution models to apply to distance-to-go signalling, introducing train- and speed-dependent train separation and brake indication points.

A mixed-integer linear programming model for conflict detection and resolution under distance-to-go signalling, obtained by integrating distance-to-go principles into the state-of-the-art RECIFE-MILP model.

A comparative analysis illustrating the operational relevance of incorporating distance-to-go principles into conflict detection and resolution modelling, as different rescheduling decisions achieving reductions in total train delay are proposed.

The paper is organised as follows. In Section 2, the state-of-the-art related to the modelling of CDR for DTG signalling is provided.

Section 3 describes the enhancement approach for CDR models to describe DTG signalling.

The mathematical formulation of the fixed-block CDR model RECIFE-MILP enhanced for DTG signalling is presented in Section 4. Section 5 presents the results of the comparative analysis. Finally, Section 6 concludes the paper. State-of-the-art in conflict detection and resolution for distance-to-go signalling In this section, we provide an overview of the state-of-the-art relevant for the topic of modelling CDR under DTG signalling. Section 2.1 focuses on DTG signalling as the de-facto standard in the development of next-generation signalling systems. Section 2.2 provides an overview on modelling approaches for CDR existing in the literature.

2.1 Distance-to-go signalling systems In the development of next-generation signalling systems, DTG is the de-facto standard. For the mainline railways, DTG signalling is included within the European Train Control System (ETCS) and the Chinese Train Control System (CTCS). For metro lines, Communication-Based Train Control (CBTC) applies DTG signalling principles. Examples of deployed DTG systems are the fixed-block ETCS Level 2 with Trackside Train Detection (TTD) and the similar CTCS Level 3. The latter is designed for the Chinese high-speed (up to 300 km/h) railway lines (Xu et al., 2017). In this paper, we focus on ETCS Level 2 with TTD, hereafter referred to as ETCS L2, which is implemented on freight and passenger railways throughout the world (European Rail Supply Industry Association, 2022).

To enable cab signalling, ETCS L2 features radio communication between a radio block centre on the trackside and the trains as follows. The radio block centre receives train position information from a train. This information supports the request for a route extension to the interlocking system. Based on safety logic and input from TTD, the interlocking system sets and locks a new route for the train. As a next step, the radio block centre updates the MA before sending it to the train. With the received MA, the train recomputes and supervises a dynamic speed profile including continuous braking curves.

Corresponding to the braking curves, the brake indication point for a train can lie anywhere along the track. The end of authority, however, is consistently set at the end of a block or TTD section (TDS). The TDSs correspond to the parts of the track in which the presence of a train is automatically detected. Whether the end of authority corresponds to a block or TDS depends on the implemented ETCS L2 variant. It can also depend on whether it is on the open line, in a station or around switches. A schematic representation of the ETCS L2 system is provided in Figure 1. In the figure, two trains at the speed-dependent minimum separation distance are included.

Figure 1: Schematic layout of the minimum separation between two trains in a speed-distance diagram under ETCS L2 with (block) section boundaries, radio block centre (RBC) and radio communication (GSM-R). The separation is related to the brake indication point (IP) and the end of authority (EoA) depending on the braking curve.

Within ETCS and CTCS, more advanced application levels are being developed, but not yet deployed.

In particular, ETCS Level 2 with onboard train integrity monitoring (TIM), previously known as ETCS Level 3. This allows the end of authority to be located at the end of the last free virtual (non-physical) block, e.g., in ETCS Level 2 Virtual Block, or even at a safety margin behind the rear position of a moving train, e.g., in ETCS Level 2 Moving Block (European Railway Agency, 2016).

function.arguments: {"description": "Conflict Detection and Resolution (CDR) MILP for railway rescheduling under ETCS Level 2 distance-to-go (DTG) signalling, enhancing the RECIFE-MILP model. Setting: a railway network with a set of trains T, a set of track resources R (block/TDS sections, with a distinction between switch resources and plain track resources), and a discrete time horizon H (e.g., minutes 0..H). Each train t follows a scheduled route through resources r in order; for each resource r on the route of train t there is a scheduled entry time a^0_{t,r} and exit time d^0_{t,r} from the original timetable. Delays may exist at the start. Speed profile options: each train t has a set of speed profile options p in P_t; each option p has a fixed running time on resource r (delta_{t,r,p}) and a speed-dependent braking/approach time before resource r (b_{t,r,p}), representing the DTG speed-dependent separation distance (brake indication point depends on train speed and braking distance). Decision variables: entry time a_{t,r} (continuous, minutes) of train t on resource r; exit time d_{t,r}; binary x_{t,r,p} = 1 if train t uses speed profile option p on resource r; binary y_{t,r} = 1 if train t occupies resource r at time theta (theta in H); binary z_{t,t',r,theta} = 1 if trains t and t' both occupy resource r at time theta (conflict indicator); binary ordering variables s_{t,t',r} = 1 if train t passes resource r before train t'. Objective: minimize total delay, sum over trains of (a_{t,first} - a^0_{t,first}) weighted by train priority weights w_t (or sum of entry delays at all resources). Constraints: (1) Time consistency: d_{t,r} = a_{t,r} + sum_p delta_{t,r,p} x_{t,r,p} for each train t, resource r on its route. (2) Speed profile choice: sum_p x_{t,r,p} = 1 for each t, r. (3) Route progression: a_{t,r_next} >= d_{t,r} + sum_p b_{t,r_next,p} x_{t,r_next,p} for consecutive resources r, r_next on the route of t (the approach/braking time before entering the next resource depends on the chosen speed profile, modelling the DTG speed-dependent brake indication point). Assumptions: fixed routes (no rerouting), discrete time horizon, running times constant per speed profile option, braking/approach times precomputed per speed profile option and train type, delays measured at first resource entry, big-M = horizon H."}

# CDR MILP for Railway Rescheduling under ETCS Level 2 DTG Signalling (Enhanced RECIFE-MILP)

## Sets and Parameters
- **T**: trains; **R**: track resources (block/TDS sections), with subset **R_sw** of switch resources
- **Route(t)**: ordered resources of train *t*; **P_t**: speed profile options of train *t*
- **a⁰_{t,r}, d⁰_{t,r}**: scheduled entry/exit times; **δ_{t,r,p}**: running time of train *t* on resource *r* under profile *p*
- **b_{t,r,p}**: speed-dependent braking/approach time before resource *r* under profile *p* (DTG brake indication point)
- **w_t**: priority weight; **D_t**: initial delay; **h_r**: minimum headway on switch resources; **H**: time horizon (also big-M); **Θ = {0,…,H}**: discrete times

## Variables
- **a_{t,r}, d_{t,r} ≥ 0**: entry / exit time of train *t* on resource *r* (0 ≤ · ≤ H)
- **x_{t,r,p} ∈ {0,1}**: 1 if train *t* uses speed profile *p* on resource *r*
- **y_{t,r,θ} ∈ {0,1}**: 1 if train *t* occupies resource *r* at time *θ*
- **z_{t,t′,r,θ} ∈ {0,1}**: 1 if trains *t*, *t′* conflict on *r* at time *θ*
- **s_{t,t′,r} ∈ {0,1}**: 1 if train *t* passes resource *r* before train *t′*

## Objective
Minimise total weighted delay:

**min Σ_t w_t · (a_{t,first(t)} − a⁰_{t,first(t)})**

## Constraints

1. **Time consistency** (running time depends on chosen profile):
 d_{t,r} = a_{t,r} + Σ_p δ_{t,r,p} · x_{t,r,p}  ∀t, r ∈ Route(t)

2. **Speed profile choice**:
 Σ_{p∈P_t} x_{t,r,p} = 1  ∀t, r ∈ Route(t)

3. **Route progression with DTG braking** (approach time before next resource is speed-dependent):
 a_{t,r_next} ≥ d_{t,r} + Σ_p b_{t,r_next,p} · x_{t,r_next,p}  ∀t, consecutive r, r_next ∈ Route(t)

4. **Initial delay**:
 a_{t,first(t)} ≥ a⁰_{t,first(t)} + D_t  ∀t

5. **Occupancy linking** (big-M linearisation of y = 1 ⟺ a ≤ θ < d):
 y_{t,r,θ} ≥ 1 − (a_{t,r} − θ)/H;  y_{t,r,θ} ≥ 1 − (θ − d_{t,r} + 1)/H
 y_{t,r,θ} ≤ 1 − (θ − d_{t,r})/H;  y_{t,r,θ} ≤ 1 + (a_{t,r} − θ)/H  ∀t, r, θ

6. **Conflict detection**:
 z_{t,t′,r,θ} ≥ y_{t,r,θ} + y_{t′,r,θ} − 1  ∀ pairs t<t′, shared r, θ

7. **Ordering / conflict resolution**:
 s_{t,t′,r} + s_{t′,t,r} = 1  ∀ pairs, shared r
 a_{t′,r} ≥ d_{t,r} − H·(1 − s_{t,t′,r})  (and symmetrically for t′ first)

8. **Switch headway** (r ∈ R_sw):
 a_{t′,r} ≥ d_{t,r} + h_r − H·(1 − s_{t,t′,r})  (and symmetric)

9. **Minimum dwell time** (optional, stations):
 d_{t,r} ≥ a_{t,r} + dwell_min_{t,r}

## Key Assumptions
- Fixed routes (no rerouting); rescheduling by retiming, reordering and speed-profile choice only.
- Running times and braking/approach times are constant per (train, resource, speed profile) — precomputed from braking curves, capturing the DTG speed-dependent separation.
- Delays measured at first resource entry; discrete time horizon H; big-M = H.
- End of authority at block/TDS boundaries; brake indication points may lie anywhere (modelled via b_{t,r,p}).

Based on your input, generate a complete, linear model with variables, objective function and constraints.

Introduction

Worldwide, railways are experiencing a continuously increasing travel demand. The existing railway networks have limited capacity and fewer and fewer extension possibilities due to the costly and land-consuming infrastructure. Especially at capacity bottlenecks such as in and around stations, extensions are often not available. To fulfil future railway demand in a different way, advanced signalling systems such as distance-to-go (DTG) systems are developed as capacityincreasing alternatives to conventional fixed-block multi-aspect signalling with automatic train protection systems.

In conventional fixed-block systems, the track is partitioned into blocks of fixed lengths which can be occupied by at most one train at a time.

The block entries are protected by trackside multi-aspect signals which indicate whether an approaching train can proceed, needs to start braking or is required to stop. The automatic train protection system supervises that the trains follow the signal aspects and intervenes when a train does not start braking after a brake indication. Hence, train separation distances are determined based on a number of blocks of fixed length.

Fixed-block DTG systems feature radio-based cab signalling and continuous braking curve supervision from the train front position to the block (or section) entry corresponding to the train’s end of movement authority (MA), i.e., the permission to move to a specific location under supervision. With this, brake indications no longer need to be provided at the entry of a block. Moreover, train separation distances become speed-dependent due to the approach distance to the first occupied block being based on the train’s absolute braking distance.

For effective railway operations, real-time traffic management is crucial. In case of small delays originating from variations in rolling stock, dwell times and driver behaviour, traffic management can apply rescheduling measures such as retiming, reordering and local rerouting to resolve track conflicts while minimising the delay propagation in the network. To support human dispatchers in taking mathematically optimised rescheduling decisions, conflict detection and resolution (CDR) models describing variants of the real-time railway traffic management or rescheduling problem are developed (Cacchiani et al., 2014; Pellegrini et al., 2014). In short, the problem can be formally described as follows: given a railway network and timetable together with delayed events, find a new timetable by rescheduling trains such that all track conflicts are resolved and total delay (or other relevant objective) is minimised.

The existing CDR models mostly refer to conventional fixed-block signalling systems. As a result, they are typically microscopic models that inherently rely on the discretisation of the track into fixed blocks. Moreover, they generally neglect changes in the speed profile to fit the adjusted timetable (Reynolds et al., 2022). Hence, these models cannot accurately capture the speed-dependent separation distances typical for DTG signalling due to the implementation of braking curve supervision (Versluis et al., 2024).

In this paper, we address the research gap regarding CDR for DTG signalling by developing a CDR model for DTG and applying it to assess the operational relevance of modelling CDR for DTG. To obtain a model that represents and identifies optimised rescheduling decisions for DTG railway operations, we propose enhancements for existing CDR models. The enhancements include the introduction of speed profile options and train blocking times considering train- and speed-dependent braking distances. These two enhancements are significant as they are crucial in enabling the modelling of train- and speed-dependent brake indication points in CDR models. As a proof of concept, we incorporate the enhancements into the state-of-the-art CDR model of RECIFE-MILP (Pellegrini et al., 2015), together with a distinction between switches and the rest of the track. The resulting model is assessed through a comparative analysis with the original one for conventional fixed-block signalling in two case studies, specifically in terms of total train delay and rescheduling decisions.

With this, the main contributions of the paper are:

A modelling approach for enhancing conflict detection and resolution models to apply to distance-to-go signalling, introducing train- and speed-dependent train separation and brake indication points.

A mixed-integer linear programming model for conflict detection and resolution under distance-to-go signalling, obtained by integrating distance-to-go principles into the state-of-the-art RECIFE-MILP model.

A comparative analysis illustrating the operational relevance of incorporating distance-to-go principles into conflict detection and resolution modelling, as different rescheduling decisions achieving reductions in total train delay are proposed.

The paper is organised as follows. In Section 2, the state-of-the-art related to the modelling of CDR for DTG signalling is provided.

Section 3 describes the enhancement approach for CDR models to describe DTG signalling.

The mathematical formulation of the fixed-block CDR model RECIFE-MILP enhanced for DTG signalling is presented in Section 4. Section 5 presents the results of the comparative analysis. Finally, Section 6 concludes the paper. State-of-the-art in conflict detection and resolution for distance-to-go signalling In this section, we provide an overview of the state-of-the-art relevant for the topic of modelling CDR under DTG signalling. Section 2.1 focuses on DTG signalling as the de-facto standard in the development of next-generation signalling systems. Section 2.2 provides an overview on modelling approaches for CDR existing in the literature.

2.1 Distance-to-go signalling systems In the development of next-generation signalling systems, DTG is the de-facto standard. For the mainline railways, DTG signalling is included within the European Train Control System (ETCS) and the Chinese Train Control System (CTCS). For metro lines, Communication-Based Train Control (CBTC) applies DTG signalling principles. Examples of deployed DTG systems are the fixed-block ETCS Level 2 with Trackside Train Detection (TTD) and the similar CTCS Level 3. The latter is designed for the Chinese high-speed (up to 300 km/h) railway lines (Xu et al., 2017). In this paper, we focus on ETCS Level 2 with TTD, hereafter referred to as ETCS L2, which is implemented on freight and passenger railways throughout the world (European Rail Supply Industry Association, 2022).

To enable cab signalling, ETCS L2 features radio communication between a radio block centre on the trackside and the trains as follows. The radio block centre receives train position information from a train. This information supports the request for a route extension to the interlocking system. Based on safety logic and input from TTD, the interlocking system sets and locks a new route for the train. As a next step, the radio block centre updates the MA before sending it to the train. With the received MA, the train recomputes and supervises a dynamic speed profile including continuous braking curves.

Corresponding to the braking curves, the brake indication point for a train can lie anywhere along the track. The end of authority, however, is consistently set at the end of a block or TTD section (TDS). The TDSs correspond to the parts of the track in which the presence of a train is automatically detected. Whether the end of authority corresponds to a block or TDS depends on the implemented ETCS L2 variant. It can also depend on whether it is on the open line, in a station or around switches. A schematic representation of the ETCS L2 system is provided in Figure 1. In the figure, two trains at the speed-dependent minimum separation distance are included.

Figure 1: Schematic layout of the minimum separation between two trains in a speed-distance diagram under ETCS L2 with (block) section boundaries, radio block centre (RBC) and radio communication (GSM-R). The separation is related to the brake indication point (IP) and the end of authority (EoA) depending on the braking curve.

Within ETCS and CTCS, more advanced application levels are being developed, but not yet deployed.

In particular, ETCS Level 2 with onboard train integrity monitoring (TIM), previously known as ETCS Level 3. This allows the end of authority to be located at the end of the last free virtual (non-physical) block, e.g., in ETCS Level 2 Virtual Block, or even at a safety margin behind the rear position of a moving train, e.g., in ETCS Level 2 Moving Block (European Railway Agency, 2016).

Model 1:
# MILP for Railway Conflict Detection & Resolution under ETCS Level 2 (Distance-to-Go)

Extends the RECIFE-MILP approach by incorporating speed profile selection with speed-dependent blocking times.

---

## 1. Sets and Indices

| Set | Description |
|---|---|
| $\mathcal{T}$ | Set of trains, index $t$ |
| $\mathcal{S}$ | Set of track sections, index $s$ |
| $\mathcal{R}_t$ | Set of admissible routes for train $t$ |
| $\mathcal{P}_t$ | Set of speed profile options for train $t$ (e.g., commercial, intermediate, slower), index $p$ |
| $\mathcal{B}_{t,r,p}$ | Ordered list of sections of route $r \in \mathcal{R}_t$ under profile $p$ |
| $\mathcal{K}_{s}$ | Set of trains traversing section $s$ (over all routes/profiles) |
| $\mathcal{W}$ | Set of switches; $\mathcal{W}(r)$ = switches used by route $r$ |
| $\mathcal{C}$ | Set of ordered train pairs potentially conflicting ($\{t,t'\}$ sharing sections) |

## 2. Parameters

| Parameter | Meaning |
|---|---|
| $b_{t,r,p,s}$ | Blocking time of train $t$ on section $s$ with route $r$, speed profile $p$ = time during which the section must be reserved (includes approach release behind brake indication point, occupation, release) |
| $a_{t,r,p,s}$ | Nominal (unconstrained) entry time of train $t$ into section $s$ (derived from timetable + kinematics under profile $p$) |
| $\sigma_{t,s}$ | Earliest feasible passage time at section $s$ (from initial delay/scheduled departure) |
| $h_t$ | Scheduled arrival/passing time of train $t$ at its destination checkpoint |
| $M$ | Big-M constant (large enough, e.g., horizon $H$) |
| $[\ell_{w}, u_{w}]$ | Optional switch occupancy window bounds (e.g., maintenance) |
| $\Delta^{max}$ | Maximum acceptable delay |

## 3. Decision Variables

| Variable | Domain | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| $x_{t,r,p} \in \{0,1\}$ | Binary | 1 if train $t$ uses route $r$ with speed profile $p$ |
| $y^{in}_{t,s} \ge 0$ | Continuous | Actual time train $t$ enters section $s$ (start of blocking) |
| $y^{out}_{t,s} \ge 0$ | Continuous | Actual time train $t$ exits section $s$ (end of blocking) |
| $z_{t,t',s} \in \{0,1\}$ | Binary | Ordering on section $s$: 1 if $t$ passes before $t'$, 0 otherwise |
| $d_t \ge 0$ | Continuous | Final delay of train $t$ |

Note: $y^{in}, y^{out}$ are only meaningful when the corresponding $x_{t,r,p}=1$ (enforced via big-M).

## 4. Objective

Minimize total (weighted) delay:

$$\min \; Z = \sum_{t \in \mathcal{T}} \omega_t \, d_t$$

with priority weights $\omega_t$ (set $\omega_t = 1$ for uniform delay).

## 5. Constraints

### 5.1 Route & speed-profile selection (exactly one option per train)

$$\sum_{r \in \mathcal{R}_t} \sum_{p \in \mathcal{P}_t} x_{t,r,p} = 1 \qquad \forall t \in \mathcal{T} \tag{1}$$

### 5.2 Link between profile choice and blocking times / nominal times

If train $t$ runs profile $p$ on route $r$, its blocking interval on section $s$ has length $b_{t,r,p,s}$ and its unconstrained timing is $a_{t,r,p,s}$:

$$y^{out}_{t,s} - y^{in}_{t,s} \ge b_{t,r,p,s} \, x_{t,r,p} - M(1 - x_{t,r,p}) \qquad \forall t, \forall r \in \mathcal{R}_t, \forall p \in \mathcal{P}_t, \forall s \in \mathcal{B}_{t,r,p} \tag{2}$$

$$y^{in}_{t,s} \ge a_{t,r,p,s}\, x_{t,r,p} - M(1-x_{t,r,p}) \qquad \forall t,r,p, s \in \mathcal{B}_{t,r,p} \tag{3}$$

(If the train does not traverse $s$, fix $y^{in}_{t,s} = y^{out}_{t,s} = 0$ or use $x$-based big-M to deactivate.)

### 5.3 Earliest passage times (respecting initial conditions)

$$y^{in}_{t,s} \ge \sigma_{t,s} \, \sum_{r,p} x_{t,r,p} \qquad \forall t, \forall s \text{ traversed by some route of } t \tag{4}$$

### 5.4 Monotone progression along the route (sequencing of sections)

For consecutive sections $s, s'$ on route $r$:

$$y^{in}_{t,s'} \ge y^{out}_{t,s} - M\!\left(1 - \sum_{p} x_{t,r,p}\right) \qquad \forall t, r, (s,s') \text{ consecutive in } \mathcal{B}_{t,r,\cdot} \tag{5}$$

### 5.5 Blocking-time conflict-freedom (section separation)

For each pair of trains $(t,t')$ and each shared section $s$, both orderings must be feasible with gap ≥ blocking times (asymmetric: leading train's exit vs. following train's approach covering its BIP):

$$y^{out}_{t,s} \le y^{in}_{t',s} - M(1 - z_{t,t',s}) \qquad \forall (t,t') \in \mathcal{C}, \; s \in \mathcal{S}_{t,t'} \tag{6a}$$

$$y^{out}_{t',s} \le y^{in}_{t,s} - M z_{t,t',s} \qquad \forall (t,t') \in \mathcal{C}, \; s \in \mathcal{S}_{t,t'} \tag{6b}$$

(The required safety margin, including the follower's braking distance behind the BIP, is embedded in $b$ and the entry times via (2)–(3).)

### 5.6 Switch separation

Two routes $r, r'$ using switch $w$ in potentially different positions conflict; enforce non-overlap on the switch:

$$y^{out}_{t,w} \le y^{in}_{t',w} - M(1 - z_{t,t',w}) \qquad \forall (t,t') \in \mathcal{C}, w \in \mathcal{W}_{t,t'} \tag{7a}$$

$$y^{out}_{t',w} \le y^{in}_{t,w} - M z_{t,t',w} \tag{7b}$$

Plus route compatibility: routes $r, r'$ through $w$ with incompatible positions cannot both be chosen:

$$x_{t,r,p} + x_{t',r',p'} \le 1 \qquad \forall \, (r,r') \text{ incompatible at some } w, \; \forall p,p' \tag{8}$$

### 5.7 Delay definition

$$y^{out}_{t,s^*_t} \le h_t + d_t \qquad \forall t \tag{9}$$

where $s^*_t$ is the final checkpoint section of train $t$. Optionally:

$$d_t \le \Delta^{max} \tag{10}$$

### 5.8 Big-M consistency

Use profile-specific $M_{t,s} = \max_{r,p}\{a_{t,r,p,s} + b_{t,r,p,s}\} - \sigma_{t,s}$ to tighten the relaxation.

---

## 6. Model Elements Explained

- **Speed profile selection (2)–(3)**: each profile $p$ implies different running times and, crucially, different **brake indication points** under distance-to-go: braking earlier/later changes the approach release portion of the blocking time $b_{t,r,p,s}$. The binaries $x_{t,r,p}$ therefore select both geometry (route) and kinematics (speed profile).
- **Blocking-time model (2), (6)**: ETCS L2 computes movement authorities so a section must stay blocked from the moment the follower's braking curve reaches the BIP until the leader clears it plus release time — captured by $[y^{in}, y^{out}]$ with length $\ge b$.
- **Ordering variables (6)–(7)**: $z$ disjuncts pairwise conflicts, exactly the RECIFE-MILP mechanism, here conditioned on the selected blocking intervals.
- **Delay objective**: total schedule deviation at destination; weighted to reflect priorities.

## 7. Assumptions (marked)

# MILP for Railway Conflict Detection & Resolution under ETCS Level 2 Distance-to-Go Signalling

## 1. Assumptions (explicitly marked)

- **A1.** Infrastructure is a set of track sections with fixed lengths; switches have fixed geometric positions connecting exactly two section pairs.
- **A2.** Each train has a set of **candidate speed profiles** (e.g., economic, standard, aggressive braking curves), each with a fixed timing pattern along its route. Higher speeds ⇒ longer **blocking times** (brake/indication/swept times grow with speed) but shorter running times.
- **A3.** Under ETCS Level 2, a train physically occupies a **block** = section itself plus its **brake indication points** (BIPs) approaching it, which may extend over upstream sections. Blocking time of section *s* for train *t* under profile *p* = time the train's Supervised Location + protection area (LSS, EBI/EBP curves) overlaps section *s*, computed from movement authority logic.
- **A4.** A train's route (sequence of sections) is fixed; only speed profile, entry/passage times, and order on shared resources are free. Microscopic kinematics are pre-computed offline per (train, profile) pair.
- **A5.** Trains cannot stop/restart outside stations (profiles are continuous-run); dwell times at stations are fixed parameters.
- **A6.** All data are deterministic and known in real time at the horizon start (rolling horizon re-solve handles uncertainty).
- **A7.** Time is discretized or handled via "big-time" continuous variables; disjunctions use big-M.

## 2. Sets and Indices

| Set | Meaning |
|---|---|
| $T$ | trains, index $t$ |
| $S$ | track sections, index $s$ |
| $P_t$ | candidate speed profiles of train $t$, index $p$ |
| $W$ | switches, index $w$ |
| $R = S \cup W$ | shared resources, index $r$ |
| $R_t \subseteq R$ | resources traversed by train $t$ (route), in order |
| $P(t,s)$ | profiles $p$ of train $t$ that traverse section $s$ |
| $W(w)$ | sections adjacent to switch $w$ |

## 3. Parameters

- $d_t$ : scheduled departure/entry time (first passage) of train $t$.
- $b^{in}_{t,s,p},\; b^{out}_{t,s,p}$ : **blocking entry/exit times** (incl. BIP extension and braking overlap) of train $t$ on section $s$ under profile $p$; $b^{out}-b^{in}$ = speed-dependent blocking time.
- $b^{in}_{t,w,p}, b^{out}_{t,w,p}$ : same for switch $w$ (occupancy + point locking + route locking).
- $\sigma_t$ : maximum admissible delay of train $t$ (e.g., ticketed connections).
- $M$ : big-M constant ($M$ = horizon length).
- $\gamma_{t,p}$ : energy/penalty cost of using profile $p$.
- $\lambda_t$ : priority weight of train $t$.
- $E_{t,p}$ : entry-time offset of the first blocking interval for profile $p$ (relative to train's reference time).

## 4. Variables

**Binary:**
- $x_{t,p} \in \{0,1\}$ : 1 if train $t$ runs speed profile $p$.
- $y^{r}_{ij} \in \{0,1\}$ for each resource $r$, each unordered pair of trains $\{i,j\}$ that both use $r$ : ordering variable, 1 if $i$ passes before $j$.
- $z^{r}_{ij} \in \{0,1\}$ : 1 if trains $i,j$ use resource $r$ **on different profiles-compatible order**, used to deactivate constraints (indicator relaxation, see §7).

**Continuous:**
- $a_t \ge 0$ : actual (optimized) entry time of train $t$.
- $e_r \ge 0$ : scheduled **blocking-entry time** of the train on resource $r$ (per train-resource: $e_{t,r}$).
- $D_t \ge 0$ : delay of train $t$ at its reference point (exit station).

## 5. Objective

$$\min \; \sum_{t \in T} \lambda_t D_t \;+\; \sum_{t\in T}\sum_{p \in P_t} \gamma_{t,p}\, x_{t,p}$$

(Delay minimization with profile-cost tie-breaking; priorities via $\lambda_t$.)

## 6. Constraints

**(C1) Profile selection — exactly one profile per train:**
$$\sum_{p \in P_t} x_{t,p} = 1 \qquad \forall t \in T$$

**(C2) Entry-time consistency with profile:**
$$a_t \ge d_t \qquad \forall t \in T$$
$$e_{t,s} \ge a_t + \sum_{p} E_{t,s,p}\, x_{t,p} \;-\; M\Big(1-\sum_p x_{t,p}\Big) \quad \text{(trivially linear; simpler:)}$$
$$e_{t,s} = a_t + \sum_{p \in P(t,s)} E_{t,s,p}\, x_{t,p} \qquad \forall t, \forall s \in R_t$$

(entry time of train $t$'s blocking interval on $s$ is a function of chosen profile and entry time $a_t$.)

**(C3) Exit time / delay definition:** let $F_{t,p}$ be the exit blocking time under profile $p$:
$$D_t \ge \Big(a_t + \sum_{p \in P_t} F_{t,p}\, x_{t,p}\Big) - \tau_t - M(1-\cdot)\;\Rightarrow\; \text{linear form:}$$
$$D_t \ge a_t + \sum_{p \in P_t} F_{t,p}x_{t,p} - \tau_t \qquad \forall t \in T$$
where $\tau_t$ = nominal arrival time; combined with $D_t \ge 0$ and the objective this yields $D_t = \max\{0,\ \text{lateness}\}$.

**(C4) Blocking-time / separation constraints on sections and switches (the core conflict constraints).**

For each resource $r$ and pair of trains $i \neq j$ both using $r$ (with $i$ on profile $p_i$, $j$ on $p_j$), the blocking intervals must not overlap. Disjunctive formulation:

*Case 1 — $i$ before $j$ ($y^{r}_{ij}=1$):*
$$e_{j,r} \;\ge\; e_{i,r} + \sum_{p_i}\big(b^{out}_{i,r,p_i} - b^{in}_{i,r,p_i}\big)x_{i,p_i} - M\big(1 - y^{r}_{ij}\big) - M\big(1 - z^{r}_{ij}\big)$$

*Case 2 — $j$ before $i$ ($y^{r}_{ij}=0$):*
$$e_{i,r} \;\ge\; e_{j,r} + \sum_{p_j}\big(b^{out}_{j,r,p_j} - b^{in}_{j,r,p_j}\big)x_{j,p_j} - M\,y^{r}_{ij} - M\big(1 - z^{r}_{ij}\big)$$

Here $z^{r}_{ij}=0$ deactivates the constraint when the pair can be proven non-conflicting (e.g., conflicting routes not simultaneously selectable), reducing the model size.

**(C5) Headway refinement (optional, closer to RECIFE-MILP):** replace single-interval blocking by a **sequence of blocking steps** (LSS, EBI, EBP sections) — apply (C4) per step $k$ with times $b^{k,in}, b^{k,out}$, i.e., one constraint pair per overlapping blocking step, ensuring the full braking-curve envelope is respected.

**(C6) Transitivity of orders along each train's route** (strengthens the LP relaxation):
$$y^{r}_{ij} + y^{r'}_{jk} - y^{r'}_{ik} \le 1 \qquad \text{for consistent triples on overlapping resources}$$

**(C7) Route/switch constraints.** For each switch $w$ with opposed sections $s_1, s_2$ (mutually exclusive routes through the switch):
$$z^{w}_{ij} \ge 1 - \sum_{p \in P_i \cap P(w,s_1)} x_{i,p} \cdot \mathbb{1}[j \text{ uses } s_2] \quad \text{(indicator linearization)}$$
Practically: for every pair of trains $(i,j)$ whose routes through $w$ are **geometrically incompatible** (opposing diverging routes):
$$e_{j,w} \ge e_{i,w} + \sum_p (b^{out}_{i,w,p}-b^{in}_{i,w,p})x_{i,p} - M(1-y^{w}_{ij})$$
$$e_{i,w} \ge e_{j,w} + \sum_p (b^{out}_{j,w,p}-b^{in}_{j,w,p})x_{j,p} - M\,y^{w}_{ij}$$
i.e., no overlap at all is allowed (no $z$ relaxation) since the switch cannot serve both routes concurrently. Additional fixed-route locking time $\ell_w$ is folded into $b^{out}_{t,w,p}$.

**(C8) Connection/initial-condition constraints (optional):**
$$a_t \ge a_{t'} + c_{t',t} \quad \text{for guaranteed connections } (t' \to t).$$

**(C9) Bounds:**
$$0 \le D_t \le \sigma_t, \qquad a_t \in [d_t,\ d_t + \sigma_t]$$

## 7. Explanation of Key Modeling Choices

- **Speed-dependence via $x_{t,p}$**: blocking times $b^{out}-b^{in}$ multiply the profile binary, so a faster profile both shortens running time and lengthens its braking envelope on approach sections — the ETCS trade-off is captured exactly.
- **BIP handling**: since a train's blocking on section $s$ may start *before* it reaches $s$ (brake indication points on $s-1, s-2,\dots$), $b^{in}_{t,s,p}$ can be earlier than the physical entry; constraints (C4) on those upstream sections implicitly forbid another train entering the braking envelope — this is precisely ETCS Level 2 distance-to-go separation.
- **Big-M disjunctions** model the "either before or after" ordering on each resource; the auxiliary $z$ variables and transitivity constraints (C6) are standard tightening devices from RECIFE-MILP.
- **Rolling horizon**: solve in real time each time a new train enters; fix orders $y$ of already-running trains to warm-start.

This model is linear in $(x, y, z, e, a, D)$ with mixed binary/continuous variables — a valid MILP solvable by branch-and-bound with LP relaxations strengthened by (C6).
