Introduction

Worldwide, railways are experiencing a continuously increasing travel demand. The existing railway networks have limited capacity and fewer and fewer extension possibilities due to the costly and land-consuming infrastructure. Especially at capacity bottlenecks such as in and around stations, extensions are often not available. To fulfil future railway demand in a different way, advanced signalling systems such as distance-to-go (DTG) systems are developed as capacityincreasing alternatives to conventional fixed-block multi-aspect signalling with automatic train protection systems.

In conventional fixed-block systems, the track is partitioned into blocks of fixed lengths which can be occupied by at most one train at a time.

The block entries are protected by trackside multi-aspect signals which indicate whether an approaching train can proceed, needs to start braking or is required to stop. The automatic train protection system supervises that the trains follow the signal aspects and intervenes when a train does not start braking after a brake indication. Hence, train separation distances are determined based on a number of blocks of fixed length.

Fixed-block DTG systems feature radio-based cab signalling and continuous braking curve supervision from the train front position to the block (or section) entry corresponding to the train’s end of movement authority (MA), i.e., the permission to move to a specific location under supervision. With this, brake indications no longer need to be provided at the entry of a block. Moreover, train separation distances become speed-dependent due to the approach distance to the first occupied block being based on the train’s absolute braking distance.

For effective railway operations, real-time traffic management is crucial. In case of small delays originating from variations in rolling stock, dwell times and driver behaviour, traffic management can apply rescheduling measures such as retiming, reordering and local rerouting to resolve track conflicts while minimising the delay propagation in the network. To support human dispatchers in taking mathematically optimised rescheduling decisions, conflict detection and resolution (CDR) models describing variants of the real-time railway traffic management or rescheduling problem are developed (Cacchiani et al., 2014; Pellegrini et al., 2014). In short, the problem can be formally described as follows: given a railway network and timetable together with delayed events, find a new timetable by rescheduling trains such that all track conflicts are resolved and total delay (or other relevant objective) is minimised.

The existing CDR models mostly refer to conventional fixed-block signalling systems. As a result, they are typically microscopic models that inherently rely on the discretisation of the track into fixed blocks. Moreover, they generally neglect changes in the speed profile to fit the adjusted timetable (Reynolds et al., 2022). Hence, these models cannot accurately capture the speed-dependent separation distances typical for DTG signalling due to the implementation of braking curve supervision (Versluis et al., 2024).

In this paper, we address the research gap regarding CDR for DTG signalling by developing a CDR model for DTG and applying it to assess the operational relevance of modelling CDR for DTG. To obtain a model that represents and identifies optimised rescheduling decisions for DTG railway operations, we propose enhancements for existing CDR models. The enhancements include the introduction of speed profile options and train blocking times considering train- and speed-dependent braking distances. These two enhancements are significant as they are crucial in enabling the modelling of train- and speed-dependent brake indication points in CDR models. As a proof of concept, we incorporate the enhancements into the state-of-the-art CDR model of RECIFE-MILP (Pellegrini et al., 2015), together with a distinction between switches and the rest of the track. The resulting model is assessed through a comparative analysis with the original one for conventional fixed-block signalling in two case studies, specifically in terms of total train delay and rescheduling decisions.

With this, the main contributions of the paper are:

A modelling approach for enhancing conflict detection and resolution models to apply to distance-to-go signalling, introducing train- and speed-dependent train separation and brake indication points.

A mixed-integer linear programming model for conflict detection and resolution under distance-to-go signalling, obtained by integrating distance-to-go principles into the state-of-the-art RECIFE-MILP model.

A comparative analysis illustrating the operational relevance of incorporating distance-to-go principles into conflict detection and resolution modelling, as different rescheduling decisions achieving reductions in total train delay are proposed.

The paper is organised as follows. In Section 2, the state-of-the-art related to the modelling of CDR for DTG signalling is provided.

Section 3 describes the enhancement approach for CDR models to describe DTG signalling.

The mathematical formulation of the fixed-block CDR model RECIFE-MILP enhanced for DTG signalling is presented in Section 4. Section 5 presents the results of the comparative analysis. Finally, Section 6 concludes the paper. State-of-the-art in conflict detection and resolution for distance-to-go signalling In this section, we provide an overview of the state-of-the-art relevant for the topic of modelling CDR under DTG signalling. Section 2.1 focuses on DTG signalling as the de-facto standard in the development of next-generation signalling systems. Section 2.2 provides an overview on modelling approaches for CDR existing in the literature.

2.1 Distance-to-go signalling systems In the development of next-generation signalling systems, DTG is the de-facto standard. For the mainline railways, DTG signalling is included within the European Train Control System (ETCS) and the Chinese Train Control System (CTCS). For metro lines, Communication-Based Train Control (CBTC) applies DTG signalling principles. Examples of deployed DTG systems are the fixed-block ETCS Level 2 with Trackside Train Detection (TTD) and the similar CTCS Level 3. The latter is designed for the Chinese high-speed (up to 300 km/h) railway lines (Xu et al., 2017). In this paper, we focus on ETCS Level 2 with TTD, hereafter referred to as ETCS L2, which is implemented on freight and passenger railways throughout the world (European Rail Supply Industry Association, 2022).

To enable cab signalling, ETCS L2 features radio communication between a radio block centre on the trackside and the trains as follows. The radio block centre receives train position information from a train. This information supports the request for a route extension to the interlocking system. Based on safety logic and input from TTD, the interlocking system sets and locks a new route for the train. As a next step, the radio block centre updates the MA before sending it to the train. With the received MA, the train recomputes and supervises a dynamic speed profile including continuous braking curves.

Corresponding to the braking curves, the brake indication point for a train can lie anywhere along the track. The end of authority, however, is consistently set at the end of a block or TTD section (TDS). The TDSs correspond to the parts of the track in which the presence of a train is automatically detected. Whether the end of authority corresponds to a block or TDS depends on the implemented ETCS L2 variant. It can also depend on whether it is on the open line, in a station or around switches. A schematic representation of the ETCS L2 system is provided in Figure 1. In the figure, two trains at the speed-dependent minimum separation distance are included.

Figure 1: Schematic layout of the minimum separation between two trains in a speed-distance diagram under ETCS L2 with (block) section boundaries, radio block centre (RBC) and radio communication (GSM-R). The separation is related to the brake indication point (IP) and the end of authority (EoA) depending on the braking curve.

Within ETCS and CTCS, more advanced application levels are being developed, but not yet deployed.

In particular, ETCS Level 2 with onboard train integrity monitoring (TIM), previously known as ETCS Level 3. This allows the end of authority to be located at the end of the last free virtual (non-physical) block, e.g., in ETCS Level 2 Virtual Block, or even at a safety margin behind the rear position of a moving train, e.g., in ETCS Level 2 Moving Block (European Railway Agency, 2016).

## 2. Sets and Parameters

| Symbol | Meaning |
|---|---|
| T | trains; R | track resources (TDS + switches) |
| Pᵢ | speed profiles of train i (nominal, faster, slower) |
| Rᵢ | alternative routes of train i; Rᵢᵣ = resources of route ρ |
| wᵢ | delay weight of train i |
| aᵢ, dᵢ | scheduled entry (origin departure) / exit (destination arrival) times |
| tᵢᵣₚ | running time of train i on r with profile p |
| dwᵢₛ | minimum dwell time of train i at station s |
| h[i,j,r,p,q] | speed-profile-dependent minimum headway |
| M | big-M constant |

## 3. Decision Variables

- eᵢᵣ, xᵢᵣ ∈ ℤ⁺ : entry / exit time of train i at resource r.
- yᵢⱼᵣ ∈ {0,1} : 1 if train i precedes train j on resource r (i before j).
- zᵢₚ ∈ {0,1} : 1 if train i uses speed profile p (∑ₚ zᵢₚ = 1).
- uᵢρ ∈ {0,1} : 1 if train i uses route ρ ∈ Rᵢ (∑ρ uᵢρ = 1).
- oᵢᵣ ∈ {0,1} : 1 if resource r is on the chosen route of train i (occupancy).
- Dᵢ ≥ 0 : delay of train i at its scheduled exit point.

## 4. Objective

Minimize total weighted delay:

**min ∑ᵢ wᵢ Dᵢ**

## 5. Constraints

**(1) Speed profile selection**

∑ₚ∈Pᵢ zᵢₚ = 1  ∀i ∈ T

**(2) Route consistency**

∑ρ∈Rᵢ uᵢρ = 1  ∀i ∈ T
oᵢᵣ = ∑ρ∈Rᵢ: r∈Rᵢρ uᵢρ  ∀i, ∀r ∈ R  (linear: r is occupied iff a chosen route contains it)

**(3) Running times (profile-dependent)**

xᵢᵣ − eᵢᵣ ≥ tᵢᵣᵐⁱⁿ − M(1 − zᵢₚ) − M(1 − oᵢᵣ)  ∀i, r, p
xᵢᵣ − eᵢᵣ ≤ tᵢᵣᵐᵃˣ + M(1 − zᵢₚ) + M(1 − oᵢᵣ)  ∀i, r, p

with tᵢᵣᵐⁱⁿ = tᵢᵣᵐᵃˣ = tᵢᵣₚ when profile p is fixed; if only one profile, drop z.

**(4) Ordering disjunctions (no-overlap on each resource, speed-dependent headways)**

For every pair i < j and every resource r, with profiles p (i) and q (j):

xᵢᵣ + h[i,j,r,p,q] − M(1 − yᵢⱼᵣ) ≤ eⱼᵣ + M(2 − zᵢₚ − zⱼq) + M(1 − oᵢᵣ) + M(1 − oⱼᵣ)
xⱼᵣ + h[j,i,r,q,p] − M·yᵢⱼᵣ ≤ eᵢᵣ + M(2 − zᵢₚ − zⱼq) + M(1 − oᵢᵣ) + M(1 − oⱼᵣ)

If both trains occupy r and i precedes j (yᵢⱼᵣ = 1), the first applies; otherwise the second. The headway h depends on both selected profiles (DTG braking-distance separation).

**(5) Route-flow (precedence along the chosen route)**

For consecutive resources r, r′ in route ρ of train i:

eᵢᵣ′ ≥ xᵢᵣ − M(1 − uᵢρ)

**(6) Switch constraints (route locking)**

For each switch resource r and each pair of conflicting movements (i, ρ) vs (j, σ), (i,ρ) ∈ C(j,σ), i ≠ j:

eⱼᵣ ≥ xᵢᵣ − M(3 − uᵢρ − uⱼσ − yᵢⱼᵣ)
eᵢᵣ ≥ xⱼᵣ − M(2 − uᵢρ − uⱼσ + yᵢⱼᵣ)

i.e., if both conflicting routes are selected, the ordering variable enforces mutual exclusion including route-locking release time (absorbed in h or added as a constant).

**(7) Timetable / delay constraints**

eᵢᵣₒᵣᵢᵍⁱⁿ ≥ dᵢ  ∀i (no early departure)
xᵢ,exit = ∑ρ uᵢρ · (scheduled exit via ρ) + Dᵢ  → linearized as:
xᵢ,exit ≥ aᵢ,ρ − M(1 − uᵢρ)  ∀ρ
Dᵢ ≥ xᵢ,exit − aᵢ,ρ − M(1 − uᵢρ)  ∀ρ
Dᵢ ≤ Dᵐᵃˣ

**(8) Dwell times at stations**

For station resources s with dwell requirement: xᵢₛ − eᵢₛ ≥ dwᵢₛ − M(1 − oᵢₛ)

**(9) Variable domains**

e, x, D ≥ 0 integer; y, z, u, o ∈ {0,1}.

## 6. Explanation of Model Elements

- **Retiming** is captured by e/x variables; **reordering** by the y binaries (big-M disjunctions, standard job-shop formulation); **rerouting** by u/o binaries selecting exactly one route per train.
- **DTG signalling** enters through the data h[i,j,r,p,q]: because the follower's EoA braking distance depends on its speed profile, separation is not a constant headway but a profile-pair-dependent parameter — the key enhancement over classical RECIFE-MILP.
- **Switches vs plain TDS**: plain resources need only constraint (4); switches additionally enforce route-locking mutual exclusion via (6).
- The model is a linear MILP (all nonlinearities precomputed into h and t parameters), solvable by branch-and-bound for real-time CR on regional networks.

If you'd like, I can instantiate this on a small example network with numeric data to show a concrete solution.

messages.content:
# MILP for Conflict Detection & Resolution (CDR) under DTG Signalling (ETCS L2)

## 1. Sets and Indices

| Symbol | Meaning |
|---|---|
| $I$ | set of trains, indexed $i, j$ |
| $R$ | set of track resources (block sections), indexed $r$ |
| $P_{ir}$ | set of running-time profiles of train $i$ on resource $r$ (e.g., speed profiles under different braking curves), indexed $p, q$ |
| $C$ | set of conflicting switch-route pairs $(r, s)$: occupying $r$ and $s$ simultaneously is not allowed (conflict graph edges) |
| $R_i \subseteq R$ | resources on the route of train $i$, in order; $r_{\text{prev}}(i,r)$ = predecessor of $r$ on $i$'s route |

## 2. Parameters

| Symbol | Meaning |
|---|---|
| $t_{irp}$ | running time of train $i$ on $r$ under profile $p$ |
| $h[i,j,r,p,q]$ | headway time between exit of $j$ and entry of $i$ on $r$ when $i$ uses profile $p$ and $j$ uses profile $q$ (asymmetric: $h[i,j,r,p,q] \neq h[j,i,r,q,p]$ in general) |
| $\ell_{rs}$ | route-locking release time for conflicting switch-route pair $(r,s)$ |
| $A_i$ | scheduled exit (arrival at destination) time of train $i$ |
| $e_i^{sched}$ | scheduled entry time of train $i$ at its origin resource |
| $\delta_i$ | initial delay of train $i$ (input) |
| $w_i \geq 0$ | delay weight of train $i$ |
| $M$ | sufficiently large constant |

## 3. Variables

| Symbol | Domain | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| $o_{ir}$ | binary | 1 if train $i$ occupies resource $r$ |
| $z_{ip}$ | binary | 1 if train $i$ selects profile $p$ (per resource: $z_{irp}$; written $z_{ip}$ per $(i,r)$ for brevity) |
| $y_{ijr}$ | binary, defined for $i<j$ | 1 if $i$ passes $r$ before $j$; $y_{jir} := 1 - y_{ijr}$ |
| $e_{ir}, x_{ir} \geq 0$ | continuous | entry / exit time of train $i$ on resource $r$ |
| $x_{i,\text{exit}} \geq 0$ | continuous | exit event of train $i$ (destination) |
| $D_i \geq 0$ | continuous | final delay of train $i$ |

## 4. Objective

$$\min \sum_{i \in I} w_i D_i \tag{OBJ}$$

## 5. Constraints

**(1) Route occupancy** — train $i$ occupies exactly the resources on its route:

$$o_{ir} = 1 \quad \forall i \in I,\ \forall r \in R_i \tag{1}$$

**(2) Profile selection** — exactly one running-time profile per occupied resource:

$$\sum_{p \in P_{ir}} z_{ip} = o_{ir} \quad \forall i \in I,\ \forall r \in R_i \tag{2}$$

**(3) Running time** (entry/exit consistency, active only when occupying $r$):

$$x_{ir} - e_{ir} \geq \sum_{p \in P_{ir}} t_{irp}\, z_{ip} - M(1 - o_{ir}) \quad \forall i, r \in R_i \tag{3a}$$

Optionally, if maximum running times apply:

$$x_{ir} - e_{ir} \leq \sum_{p \in P_{ir}} t_{irp}\, z_{ip} + s_{ir} + M(1 - o_{ir}) \quad \forall i, r \in R_i \tag{3b}$$

with slack variable $s_{ir} \geq 0$ (dwell/holding allowed on the resource).

**(4) Headway / ordering on each resource** — for each pair $i<j$, resource $r \in R_i \cap R_j$, and profile pair $(p,q)$, enforce exactly one of the two orderings; the constraint is active **only** when both trains occupy $r$ **and** the respective profiles are selected:

$$x_{ir} + h[i,j,r,p,q] \leq e_{jr} + M\,y_{ijr} + M(1-o_{ir}) + M(1-o_{jr}) + M(1-z_{ip}) + M(1-z_{jq}) \tag{4a}$$

$$x_{jr} + h[j,i,r,q,p] \leq e_{ir} + M(1-y_{ijr}) + M(1-o_{ir}) + M(1-o_{jr}) + M(1-z_{ip}) + M(1-z_{jq}) \tag{4b}$$

Since $y_{jir} = 1 - y_{ijr}$, exactly one of (4a)/(4b) is binding whenever both trains occupy $r$ with profiles $p$ and $q$ selected; otherwise the big-M terms relax it.

**(5) Route continuity** — consecutive resources on a route, active only when both are occupied:

$$e_{ir} \geq x_{i,r_{\text{prev}}(i,r)} - M(2 - o_{ir} - o_{i,r_{\text{prev}}(i,r)}) \quad \forall i,\ r \in R_i,\ r_{\text{prev}}(i,r) \neq \emptyset \tag{5}$$

Also $e_{ir}, x_{ir} \geq 0$ always; all timing constraints are relaxed by $o$ when the resource is not occupied.

**(6) Switch conflicts** — for each conflicting pair $(r,s) \in C$ and each pair of trains $i \neq j$ occupying them, mutual exclusion with route-locking release time $\ell_{rs}$; a single ordering binary $g_{ij}^{rs}$ (for $i<j$) decides which train is released first:

$$x_{ir} + \ell_{rs} \leq e_{js} + M\,g_{ij}^{rs} + M(1-o_{ir}) + M(1-o_{js}) \tag{6a}$$

$$x_{js} + \ell_{rs} \leq e_{ir} + M(1-g_{ij}^{rs}) + M(1-o_{js}) + M(1-o_{ir}) \tag{6b}$$

$$g_{ij}^{rs} \in \{0,1\} \tag{6c}$$

(Analogous constraints for the pair $(s,r)$ if both directions of the conflict graph are enumerated, or symmetrically with roles of $r,s$ swapped.)

**(7) Exit event and final delay** — single exit event per train, no early arrival:

$$x_{i,\text{exit}} \geq A_i \quad \forall i \in I \tag{7a}$$

$$D_i \geq x_{i,\text{exit}} - A_i \quad \forall i \in I \tag{7b}$$

$$D_i \geq 0 \tag{7c}$$

**(8) Initial conditions** — trains enter at their delayed actual entry time:

$$e_{i,\text{origin}(i)} = e_i^{sched} + \delta_i \quad \forall i \in I \tag{8}$$

## 6. Assumptions

1. **Routes are fixed inputs** ($R_i$ given); only timing and ordering are decided. Route choice would require additional binaries.
2. **DTG/ETCS L2 semantics**: each block section (resource) is exclusively occupied; headway $h$ depends on both trains' speed/braking profiles, hence the profile pair $(p,q)$ dependence.
3. **Profiles**: exactly one profile per (train, resource); profiles capture different deceleration/braking-curve behaviour, giving resource-dependent running and headway times.
4. **Switch conflicts** are precomputed as a conflict graph $C$; $\ell_{rs}$ models the route-locking release time before the conflicting route can be locked again.
5. **Big-M** must dominate any feasible time difference (e.g., $M \geq \max_i(A_i + \delta_i + \sum t) - \min_i e_i^{sched}$ plus all headways).
6. **Delays** are measured only at the destination exit event; early arrival is not allowed ($x_{i,\text{exit}} \geq A_i$), so $D_i$ correctly captures lateness.
7. **No overtaking within a resource** is implied by (4); overtaking across resources is possible if the $y$ orderings differ between consecutive resources.
8. All times are continuous (minutes or seconds); the model is a pure MILP with binaries $o, z, y, g$ and continuous $e, x, D, s$.

Route continuity (5) must then be conditioned on the chosen route: e_{ir} ≥ x_{i,r'} − M(1 − u_{iρ}) for consecutive r', r on route ρ. 2. In (4), the headway h[i,j,r,p,q] should be defined explicitly for DTG: h = (braking distance of follower j under profile q to the EoA at end of r)/speed + safety margin + TDS length + train length j, minus any credit from leader i's braking distance — state this as precomputed data.

3. Add dwell-time constraints at station resources: x_{is} − e_{is} ≥ dw_{is} − M(1 − o_{is}).

4. Keep objective min Σ w_i D_i and all assumptions; produce the complete final model with numbered constraints."}

messages.content:
# CDR MILP under DTG Signalling — Final Model

## Sets and indices
- $i, j \in T$: trains
- $r, r' \in R$: track resources (segments); $s \in S \subseteq R$: station resources
- $p, q \in P$: running profiles (speed profiles)
- $\rho \in \mathcal{R}_i$: candidate routes of train $i$
- $R_i \subseteq R$: resources usable by train $i$

## Precomputed data
- $br_{jq}$: braking distance of train $j$ under profile $q$ (m)
- $L_j$: length of train $j$ (m); $TDS_r$: train detection system length of resource $r$ (m)
- $m_{safety}$: safety margin (m); $v_{jq}$: speed of train $j$ under profile $q$ (m/s)
- **DTG headway (precomputed, per feedback item 2):**

$$h[i,j,r,p,q] = \frac{br_{jq}^{EoA(r)}}{v_{jq}} + m_{safety}/v_{jq} + TDS_r/v_{jq} + L_j/v_{jq} - \frac{br_{ip}^{EoA(r)}}{v_{ip}}$$

i.e. time for follower $j$ (profile $q$) to brake from its speed to the End of Authority at the end of $r$, plus safety margin, plus the TDS (track-section) length, plus train length $j$, **minus the credit** from leader $i$'s braking distance (leader braking closer to the EoA reduces required separation).
- $dw_{is}$: minimum dwell time of train $i$ at station $s$
- $M$: big-M; $w_i$: delay weight; $a_i$: ideal (unconstrained) exit time

## Variables
- $x_{ir} \ge 0$: entry (occupation start) time of train $i$ on resource $r$
- $e_{ir} \ge 0$: exit (release) time of train $i$ on resource $r$
- $o_{ir} \in \{0,1\}$: 1 if train $i$ occupies resource $r$
- $u_{i\rho} \in \{0,1\}$: 1 if train $i$ uses route $\rho \in \mathcal{R}_i$
- $D_i \ge 0$: delay of train $i$

## Model

**Objective (1):**
$$\min \sum_{i \in T} w_i D_i$$

**Route selection (2):**
$$\sum_{\rho \in \mathcal{R}_i} u_{i\rho} = 1 \qquad \forall i \in T$$

**Occupancy–route linking (3):**
$$o_{ir} = \sum_{\rho \in \mathcal{R}_i:\, r \in \rho} u_{i\rho} \qquad \forall i \in T,\ \forall r \in R_i$$

**Route continuity, conditioned on chosen route (4):**
$$e_{ir'} \le x_{ir}, \qquad e_{ir'} \ge x_{ir} - M(1 - u_{i\rho}) \qquad \forall i,\ \forall \rho \in \mathcal{R}_i,\ \forall (r', r) \text{ consecutive on } \rho$$

**Resource occupancy duration (5):**
$$e_{ir} \ge x_{ir} + \tau_{irp} - M(1 - o_{ir}) \qquad \forall i,\ r \in R_i,\ p \in P$$

**Dwell time at stations (6):**
$$x_{is} - e_{is} \ge dw_{is} - M(1 - o_{is}) \qquad \forall i \in T,\ \forall s \in S \cap R_i$$

**DTG headway / no-overlap (7):** for each ordered pair $(i,j)$, $i \ne j$, common resource $r$, profiles $p, q$:
$$x_{jr} \ge e_{ir} + h[i,j,r,p,q] - M(3 - o_{ir} - o_{jr} - y_{ijrp})$$
$$x_{ir} \ge e_{jr} + h[j,i,r,q,p] - M(4 - o_{ir} - o_{jr} - y_{ijrp})$$
$$y_{ijrp} \le o_{ir}, \quad y_{ijrp} \le o_{jr}, \quad y_{ijrp} \ge o_{ir} + o_{jr} - 1 \qquad \forall i<j,\ r,\ p$$
with $y_{ijrp} \in \{0,1\}$ indicating both trains occupy $r$ (ordering enforced in one direction only when both present).

**Delay definition (8):**
$$D_i \ge x_{i, r_i^{last}} - a_i, \qquad D_i \ge 0 \qquad \forall i \in T$$

**Variable domains (9):**
$$x_{ir}, e_{ir} \ge 0;\quad o_{ir}, u_{i\rho}, y_{ijrp} \in \{0,1\};\quad D_i \ge 0$$

## Explanation of elements
- **(2)–(3)** reintroduce local rerouting: each train picks exactly one route; occupancy variables are then determined by the route choice, so all resource-based constraints automatically apply only to resources on the chosen route.
- **(4)** enforces that consecutive resources on the *chosen* route are traversed in order (exit from $r'$ before/at entry to $r$); the big-M deactivates the constraint for routes not selected.
- **(5)** links running time $\tau_{irp}$ (profile-dependent) to occupancy; inactive if $r$ not occupied.
- **(6)** enforces minimum dwell at stations, active only when the station is on the chosen route.
- **(7)** implements DTG separation: the follower may enter $r$ only after the leader releases it plus the precomputed headway $h$, which accounts for braking-to-EoA time, safety margin, TDS length, follower train length, and subtracts the leader's braking-distance credit. The $y$ variables activate the constraint only when both trains occupy $r$.
- **(8)–(9)** define weighted delay relative to ideal times and complete the domain specification.

messages.content:
# CDR MILP under DTG Signalling (ETCS L2 with TTD) — Definitive Model

## 1. Sets and Indices

| Symbol | Meaning |
|---|---|
| $I$ | set of trains, indexed $i, j$ |
| $R$ | set of track resources (block sections / TTD sections), indexed $r, s$ |
| $P_i$ | set of running-time profiles (DTG speed profiles) available to train $i$, indexed $p, q$ |
| $\mathcal{R}_i$ | set of admissible routes for train $i$ through the network, indexed $\rho$; each route is an ordered sequence of resources |
| $C$ | set of conflicting switch-route pairs $(r,s)$: occupying $r$ locks $s$ until release |
| $E$ | set of consecutive resource pairs $(r, r')$ on routes (for continuity) |
| $i < j$ | fixed total ordering on train pairs used for ordering binaries |

## 2. Parameters

| Symbol | Meaning |
|---|---|
| $e_i^{sched}$ | scheduled departure time of train $i$ at its origin |
| $\delta_i$ | initial delay of train $i$ at origin (given) |
| $A_i$ | earliest allowed arrival time of train $i$ at its exit resource |
| $w_i$ | delay weight of train $i$ |
| $D_i^{dwell}(r)$ | minimum dwell time of train $i$ at station resource $r$ |
| $\tau_{irp}$ | pure running time of train $i$ over resource $r$ under profile $p$ |
| $br_{ip}^{EoA(r)}$ | braking distance of train $i$ under profile $p$ to End-of-Authority at resource $r$ |
| $v_{ip}$ | speed of train $i$ under profile $p$ |
| $m_{safety}$ | safety margin (time-equivalent) |
| $TDS_r$ | TTD section update delay at resource $r$ |
| $L_j$ | train length of train $j$ |
| $\ell_{rs}$ | route-locking release time for conflicting pair $(r,s)$ |
| $h[i,j,r,p,q]$ | DTG headway (see Constraint (7) definition below) |
| $M$ | sufficiently large big-M constant |
| $origin(i)$, $exit(i)$ | origin / exit resource of train $i$ |

**Headway definition (explicit, per item 5):**

$$h[i,j,r,p,q] \;=\; \frac{br_{jq}^{EoA(r)} + m_{safety} + TDS_r + L_j}{v_{jq}} \;-\; \frac{br_{ip}^{EoA(r)}}{v_{ip}}$$

This is the minimum time separation between train $i$ entering $r$ (profile $p$) and follower $j$ entering $r$ (profile $q$), accounting for the follower's braking distance to the EoA, the safety margin, the TTD update delay, and the leader's train length.

## 3. Variables

**Binary:**
- $z_{ip} \in \{0,1\}$: train $i$ uses running-time profile $p$.
- $u_{i\rho} \in \{0,1\}$: train $i$ is assigned route $\rho$.
- $o_{ir} \in \{0,1\}$: train $i$ occupies resource $r$.
- $y_{ijr} \in \{0,1\}$, for $i<j$ and $r \in R$: pure ordering variable — equals 1 if $i$ passes $r$ before $j$ (no occupancy semantics attached).
- $g_{ij}^{rs} \in \{0,1\}$, for $(r,s) \in C$, $i \neq j$: ordering of the two trains at the conflicting switch pair.

**Continuous (non-negative):**
- $x_{ir} \ge 0$: time train $i$ enters resource $r$.
- $e_{ir} \ge 0$: time train $i$ releases (exits) resource $r$.
- $D_i \ge 0$: total delay of train $i$ at its exit.

## 4. Objective

$$\min \; Z = \sum_{i \in I} w_i \, D_i$$

## 5. Constraints

**(1) Profile selection** — each train uses exactly one DTG profile:
$$\sum_{p \in P_i} z_{ip} = 1 \qquad \forall i \in I$$

**(2) Route selection** — each train uses exactly one route:
$$\sum_{\rho \in \mathcal{R}_i} u_{i\rho} = 1 \qquad \forall i \in I$$

**(3) Occupancy linking** — train $i$ occupies $r$ iff a chosen route contains $r$:
$$o_{ir} = \sum_{\rho \in \mathcal{R}_i:\, r \in \rho} u_{i\rho} \qquad \forall i \in I,\; r \in R$$

**(4) Route continuity** — if train $i$ takes route $\rho$, exit from a resource precedes entry into the next resource on that route:
$$e_{ir'} \le x_{ir} + M(1 - u_{i\rho}) \qquad \forall i \in I,\; \rho \in \mathcal{R}_i,\; (r,r') \text{ consecutive on } \rho$$

**(5) Initial conditions** — entry at origin equals scheduled time plus initial delay:
$$x_{i,\,origin(i)} = e_i^{sched} + \delta_i \qquad \forall i \in I$$

**(6) Running time** — release time follows entry plus the profile-dependent running time, active only when the train actually occupies the resource:
$$e_{ir} \ge x_{ir} + \sum_{p \in P_i} \tau_{irp}\, z_{ip} - M(1 - o_{ir}) \qquad \forall i \in I,\; r \in R$$

**(7) Headway (DTG-based)** — for every pair $i<j$, every common resource $r$, and every profile pair $(p,q) \in P_i \times P_j$:

If $i$ goes first ($y_{ijr}=1$):
$$x_{jr} \ge e_{ir} + h[i,j,r,p,q] - M(1 - y_{ijr}) - M(1 - o_{ir}) - M(1 - o_{jr}) - M(1 - z_{ip}) - M(1 - z_{jq})$$

If $j$ goes first ($y_{ijr}=0$):
$$x_{ir} \ge e_{jr} + h[j,i,r,q,p] - M\,y_{ijr} - M(1 - o_{ir}) - M(1 - o_{jr}) - M(1 - z_{ip}) - M(1 - z_{jq})$$

$\forall i<j,\; r \in R \text{ common to both routes},\; p \in P_i,\; q \in P_j$.

The constraint is relaxed unless both trains occupy $r$ (via $o_{ir}, o_{jr}$) and the corresponding profiles are selected ($z_{ip}, z_{jq}$); the ordering binary $y_{ijr}$ selects which of the two inequalities is enforced.

**(8) Switch conflict / route locking** — for each conflicting switch pair $(r,s) \in C$ and trains $i \neq j$:

$$x_{js} \ge e_{ir} + \ell_{rs} - M\, g_{ij}^{rs} - M(1 - o_{ir}) - M(1 - o_{js})$$
$$x_{is} \ge e_{jr} + \ell_{rs} - M(1 - g_{ij}^{rs}) - M(1 - o_{ir}) - M(1 - o_{js})$$

$\forall (r,s) \in C,\; \forall i \neq j \in I$. If both trains occupy the respective resources, $g_{ij}^{rs}$ decides which train passes first; the other must wait until the first releases $r$ plus the release time $\ell_{rs}$.

**(9) Dwell times** — minimum dwell at station resources:
$$e_{ir} \ge x_{ir} + D_i^{dwell}(r) - M(1 - o_{ir}) \qquad \forall i \in I,\; r \in R \text{ with } D_i^{dwell}(r) > 0$$

**(10) No early arrival at exit:**
$$x_{i,\,exit(i)} \ge A_i \qquad \forall i \in I$$

**(11) Delay definition:**
$$D_i \ge x_{i,\,exit(i)} - A_i \qquad \forall i \in I$$
$$D_i \ge 0 \qquad \forall i \in I$$

**(12) Variable domains:**
$$z_{ip},\, u_{i\rho},\, o_{ir},\, y_{ijr},\, g_{ij}^{rs} \in \{0,1\}; \qquad x_{ir},\, e_{ir},\, D_i \ge 0$$

## 6. Assumptions

1. **Fixed total order $i<j$** on trains is used only to index the ordering binaries $y_{ijr}$; both directions of passing are covered by the two inequalities in (7).
2. **$y_{ijr}$ is a pure ordering variable**: it carries no occupancy semantics; it is only relaxed/enforced through the big-M structure of (7). No additional linking constraint to $o_{ir}$ is needed.
3. **Big-M validity**: $M$ must exceed any feasible time span (e.g., $M = \max_i (e_i^{sched} + \delta_i) + \sum$ of all running/dwell times + all headways).
4. **Common resources**: headway constraints (7) are generated only for resources $r$ appearing in admissible routes of both trains; likewise (8) only for trains whose routes can contain the conflicting resources.
5. **DTG profiles** $\tau_{irp}$, $br_{ip}^{EoA(r)}$, $v_{ip}$ are precomputed offline from the DTG (speed/distance profile) under ETCS L2 with TTD; the headway $h[i,j,r,p,q]$ is a parameter, not a variable.
6. **TTD granularity**: resources $r$ are TTD sections; $TDS_r$ captures the position-report/update delay of the train detection system.
7. **Route locking**: a route through switch resource $r$ locks conflicting resource $s$ until the train releases $r$ plus $\ell_{rs}$ (Constraint (8)).
8. **Delay** is measured at the exit resource against the earliest allowed arrival $A_i$; since the objective minimizes weighted $D_i$, Constraint (11) makes $D_i = \max(0, x_{i,exit} - A_i)$ at optimum.
9. **Single-threaded passage**: each train enters each resource on its route exactly once (no re-entry), consistent with the route sequences in $\mathcal{R}_i$.

response.content:
# MILP for Conflict Detection & Resolution (CDR) under DTG Signalling (ETCS L2)

## 1. Sets and Indices

| Symbol | Meaning |
|---|---|
| $I$ | set of trains, indexed $i, j$ |
| $R$ | set of track resources (block sections), indexed $r$ |
| $P_{ir}$ | set of running-time profiles of train $i$ on resource $r$ (e.g., speed profiles under different braking curves), indexed $p, q$ |
| $C$ | set of conflicting switch-route pairs $(r, s)$: occupying $r$ and $s$ simultaneously is not allowed (conflict graph edges) |
| $R_i \subseteq R$ | resources on the route of train $i$, in order; $r_{\text{prev}}(i,r)$ = predecessor of $r$ on $i$'s route |

## 2. Parameters

| Symbol | Meaning |
|---|---|
| $t_{irp}$ | running time of train $i$ on $r$ under profile $p$ |
| $h[i,j,r,p,q]$ | headway time between exit of $j$ and entry of $i$ on $r$ when $i$ uses profile $p$ and $j$ uses profile $q$ (asymmetric: $h[i,j,r,p,q] \neq h[j,i,r,q,p]$ in general) |
| $\ell_{rs}$ | route-locking release time for conflicting switch-route pair $(r,s)$ |
| $A_i$ | scheduled exit (arrival at destination) time of train $i$ |
| $e_i^{sched}$ | scheduled entry time of train $i$ at its origin resource |
| $\delta_i$ | initial delay of train $i$ (input) |
| $w_i \geq 0$ | delay weight of train $i$ |
| $M$ | sufficiently large constant |

## 3. Variables

| Symbol | Domain | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| $o_{ir}$ | binary | 1 if train $i$ occupies resource $r$ |
| $z_{ip}$ | binary | 1 if train $i$ selects profile $p$ (per resource: $z_{irp}$; written $z_{ip}$ per $(i,r)$ for brevity) |
| $y_{ijr}$ | binary, defined for $i<j$ | 1 if $i$ passes $r$ before $j$; $y_{jir} := 1 - y_{ijr}$ |
| $e_{ir}, x_{ir} \geq 0$ | continuous | entry / exit time of train $i$ on resource $r$ |
| $x_{i,\text{exit}} \geq 0$ | continuous | exit event of train $i$ (destination) |
| $D_i \geq 0$ | continuous | final delay of train $i$ |

## 4. Objective

$$\min \sum_{i \in I} w_i D_i \tag{OBJ}$$

## 5. Constraints

**(1) Route occupancy** — train $i$ occupies exactly the resources on its route:

$$o_{ir} = 1 \quad \forall i \in I,\ \forall r \in R_i \tag{1}$$

**(2) Profile selection** — exactly one running-time profile per occupied resource:

$$\sum_{p \in P_{ir}} z_{ip} = o_{ir} \quad \forall i \in I,\ \forall r \in R_i \tag{2}$$

**(3) Running time** (entry/exit consistency, active only when occupying $r$):

$$x_{ir} - e_{ir} \geq \sum_{p \in P_{ir}} t_{irp}\, z_{ip} - M(1 - o_{ir}) \quad \forall i, r \in R_i \tag{3a}$$

Optionally, if maximum running times apply:

$$x_{ir} - e_{ir} \leq \sum_{p \in P_{ir}} t_{irp}\, z_{ip} + s_{ir} + M(1 - o_{ir}) \quad \forall i, r \in R_i \tag{3b}$$

with slack variable $s_{ir} \geq 0$ (dwell/holding allowed on the resource).

**(4) Headway / ordering on each resource** — for each pair $i<j$, resource $r \in R_i \cap R_j$, and profile pair $(p,q)$, enforce exactly one of the two orderings; the constraint is active **only** when both trains occupy $r$ **and** the respective profiles are selected:

$$x_{ir} + h[i,j,r,p,q] \leq e_{jr} + M\,y_{ijr} + M(1-o_{ir}) + M(1-o_{jr}) + M(1-z_{ip}) + M(1-z_{jq}) \tag{4a}$$

$$x_{jr} + h[j,i,r,q,p] \leq e_{ir} + M(1-y_{ijr}) + M(1-o_{ir}) + M(1-o_{jr}) + M(1-z_{ip}) + M(1-z_{jq}) \tag{4b}$$

Since $y_{jir} = 1 - y_{ijr}$, exactly one of (4a)/(4b) is binding whenever both trains occupy $r$ with profiles $p$ and $q$ selected; otherwise the big-M terms relax it.

**(5) Route continuity** — consecutive resources on a route, active only when both are occupied:

$$e_{ir} \geq x_{i,r_{\text{prev}}(i,r)} - M(2 - o_{ir} - o_{i,r_{\text{prev}}(i,r)}) \quad \forall i,\ r \in R_i,\ r_{\text{prev}}(i,r) \neq \emptyset \tag{5}$$

Also $e_{ir}, x_{ir} \geq 0$ always; all timing constraints are relaxed by $o$ when the resource is not occupied.

**(6) Switch conflicts** — for each conflicting pair $(r,s) \in C$ and each pair of trains $i \neq j$ occupying them, mutual exclusion with route-locking release time $\ell_{rs}$; a single ordering binary $g_{ij}^{rs}$ (for $i<j$) decides which train is released first:

$$x_{ir} + \ell_{rs} \leq e_{js} + M\,g_{ij}^{rs} + M(1-o_{ir}) + M(1-o_{js}) \tag{6a}$$

$$x_{js} + \ell_{rs} \leq e_{ir} + M(1-g_{ij}^{rs}) + M(1-o_{js}) + M(1-o_{ir}) \tag{6b}$$

$$g_{ij}^{rs} \in \{0,1\} \tag{6c}$$

(Analogous constraints for the pair $(s,r)$ if both directions of the conflict graph are enumerated, or symmetrically with roles of $r,s$ swapped.)

**(7) Exit event and final delay** — single exit event per train, no early arrival:

$$x_{i,\text{exit}} \geq A_i \quad \forall i \in I \tag{7a}$$

$$D_i \geq x_{i,\text{exit}} - A_i \quad \forall i \in I \tag{7b}$$

$$D_i \geq 0 \tag{7c}$$

**(8) Initial conditions** — trains enter at their delayed actual entry time:

$$e_{i,\text{origin}(i)} = e_i^{sched} + \delta_i \quad \forall i \in I \tag{8}$$

## 6. Assumptions

1. **Routes are fixed inputs** ($R_i$ given); only timing and ordering are decided. Route choice would require additional binaries.
2. **DTG/ETCS L2 semantics**: each block section (resource) is exclusively occupied; headway $h$ depends on both trains' speed/braking profiles, hence the profile pair $(p,q)$ dependence.
3. **Profiles**: exactly one profile per (train, resource); profiles capture different deceleration/braking-curve behaviour, giving resource-dependent running and headway times.
4. **Switch conflicts** are precomputed as a conflict graph $C$; $\ell_{rs}$ models the route-locking release time before the conflicting route can be locked again.
5. **Big-M** must dominate any feasible time difference (e.g., $M \geq \max_i(A_i + \delta_i + \sum t) - \min_i e_i^{sched}$ plus all headways).
6. **Delays** are measured only at the destination exit event; early arrival is not allowed ($x_{i,\text{exit}} \geq A_i$), so $D_i$ correctly captures lateness.
7. **No overtaking within a resource** is implied by (4); overtaking across resources is possible if the $y$ orderings differ between consecutive resources.
8. All times are continuous (minutes or seconds); the model is a pure MILP with binaries $o, z, y, g$ and continuous $e, x, D, s$.

Introduction

Worldwide, railways are experiencing a continuously increasing travel demand. The existing railway networks have limited capacity and fewer and fewer extension possibilities due to the costly and land-consuming infrastructure. Especially at capacity bottlenecks such as in and around stations, extensions are often not available. To fulfil future railway demand in a different way, advanced signalling systems such as distance-to-go (DTG) systems are developed as capacityincreasing alternatives to conventional fixed-block multi-aspect signalling with automatic train protection systems.

In conventional fixed-block systems, the track is partitioned into blocks of fixed lengths which can be occupied by at most one train at a time.

The block entries are protected by trackside multi-aspect signals which indicate whether an approaching train can proceed, needs to start braking or is required to stop. The automatic train protection system supervises that the trains follow the signal aspects and intervenes when a train does not start braking after a brake indication. Hence, train separation distances are determined based on a number of blocks of fixed length.

Fixed-block DTG systems feature radio-based cab signalling and continuous braking curve supervision from the train front position to the block (or section) entry corresponding to the train’s end of movement authority (MA), i.e., the permission to move to a specific location under supervision. With this, brake indications no longer need to be provided at the entry of a block. Moreover, train separation distances become speed-dependent due to the approach distance to the first occupied block being based on the train’s absolute braking distance.

For effective railway operations, real-time traffic management is crucial. In case of small delays originating from variations in rolling stock, dwell times and driver behaviour, traffic management can apply rescheduling measures such as retiming, reordering and local rerouting to resolve track conflicts while minimising the delay propagation in the network. To support human dispatchers in taking mathematically optimised rescheduling decisions, conflict detection and resolution (CDR) models describing variants of the real-time railway traffic management or rescheduling problem are developed (Cacchiani et al., 2014; Pellegrini et al., 2014). In short, the problem can be formally described as follows: given a railway network and timetable together with delayed events, find a new timetable by rescheduling trains such that all track conflicts are resolved and total delay (or other relevant objective) is minimised.

The existing CDR models mostly refer to conventional fixed-block signalling systems. As a result, they are typically microscopic models that inherently rely on the discretisation of the track into fixed blocks. Moreover, they generally neglect changes in the speed profile to fit the adjusted timetable (Reynolds et al., 2022). Hence, these models cannot accurately capture the speed-dependent separation distances typical for DTG signalling due to the implementation of braking curve supervision (Versluis et al., 2024).

In this paper, we address the research gap regarding CDR for DTG signalling by developing a CDR model for DTG and applying it to assess the operational relevance of modelling CDR for DTG. To obtain a model that represents and identifies optimised rescheduling decisions for DTG railway operations, we propose enhancements for existing CDR models. The enhancements include the introduction of speed profile options and train blocking times considering train- and speed-dependent braking distances. These two enhancements are significant as they are crucial in enabling the modelling of train- and speed-dependent brake indication points in CDR models. As a proof of concept, we incorporate the enhancements into the state-of-the-art CDR model of RECIFE-MILP (Pellegrini et al., 2015), together with a distinction between switches and the rest of the track. The resulting model is assessed through a comparative analysis with the original one for conventional fixed-block signalling in two case studies, specifically in terms of total train delay and rescheduling decisions.

With this, the main contributions of the paper are:

A modelling approach for enhancing conflict detection and resolution models to apply to distance-to-go signalling, introducing train- and speed-dependent train separation and brake indication points.

A mixed-integer linear programming model for conflict detection and resolution under distance-to-go signalling, obtained by integrating distance-to-go principles into the state-of-the-art RECIFE-MILP model.

A comparative analysis illustrating the operational relevance of incorporating distance-to-go principles into conflict detection and resolution modelling, as different rescheduling decisions achieving reductions in total train delay are proposed.

The paper is organised as follows. In Section 2, the state-of-the-art related to the modelling of CDR for DTG signalling is provided.

Section 3 describes the enhancement approach for CDR models to describe DTG signalling.

The mathematical formulation of the fixed-block CDR model RECIFE-MILP enhanced for DTG signalling is presented in Section 4. Section 5 presents the results of the comparative analysis. Finally, Section 6 concludes the paper. State-of-the-art in conflict detection and resolution for distance-to-go signalling In this section, we provide an overview of the state-of-the-art relevant for the topic of modelling CDR under DTG signalling. Section 2.1 focuses on DTG signalling as the de-facto standard in the development of next-generation signalling systems. Section 2.2 provides an overview on modelling approaches for CDR existing in the literature.

2.1 Distance-to-go signalling systems In the development of next-generation signalling systems, DTG is the de-facto standard. For the mainline railways, DTG signalling is included within the European Train Control System (ETCS) and the Chinese Train Control System (CTCS). For metro lines, Communication-Based Train Control (CBTC) applies DTG signalling principles. Examples of deployed DTG systems are the fixed-block ETCS Level 2 with Trackside Train Detection (TTD) and the similar CTCS Level 3. The latter is designed for the Chinese high-speed (up to 300 km/h) railway lines (Xu et al., 2017). In this paper, we focus on ETCS Level 2 with TTD, hereafter referred to as ETCS L2, which is implemented on freight and passenger railways throughout the world (European Rail Supply Industry Association, 2022).

To enable cab signalling, ETCS L2 features radio communication between a radio block centre on the trackside and the trains as follows. The radio block centre receives train position information from a train. This information supports the request for a route extension to the interlocking system. Based on safety logic and input from TTD, the interlocking system sets and locks a new route for the train. As a next step, the radio block centre updates the MA before sending it to the train. With the received MA, the train recomputes and supervises a dynamic speed profile including continuous braking curves.

Corresponding to the braking curves, the brake indication point for a train can lie anywhere along the track. The end of authority, however, is consistently set at the end of a block or TTD section (TDS). The TDSs correspond to the parts of the track in which the presence of a train is automatically detected. Whether the end of authority corresponds to a block or TDS depends on the implemented ETCS L2 variant. It can also depend on whether it is on the open line, in a station or around switches. A schematic representation of the ETCS L2 system is provided in Figure 1. In the figure, two trains at the speed-dependent minimum separation distance are included.

Figure 1: Schematic layout of the minimum separation between two trains in a speed-distance diagram under ETCS L2 with (block) section boundaries, radio block centre (RBC) and radio communication (GSM-R). The separation is related to the brake indication point (IP) and the end of authority (EoA) depending on the braking curve.

Within ETCS and CTCS, more advanced application levels are being developed, but not yet deployed.

In particular, ETCS Level 2 with onboard train integrity monitoring (TIM), previously known as ETCS Level 3. This allows the end of authority to be located at the end of the last free virtual (non-physical) block, e.g., in ETCS Level 2 Virtual Block, or even at a safety margin behind the rear position of a moving train, e.g., in ETCS Level 2 Moving Block (European Railway Agency, 2016).

{"description": "Develop a MILP for real-time railway conflict detection and resolution (CDR) under distance-to-go (DTG) signalling (ETCS Level 2 with trackside train detection), enhancing the RECIFE-MILP model. 

Setting: A railway line/network divided into fixed TTD sections (blocks/TDS). Trains follow a given reference timetable; some trains are delayed. We must reschedule trains (retiming, reordering, local rerouting) so that all conflicts on track resources are resolved, respecting DTG signalling: train separation distances are speed-dependent because the brake indication point is determined by the train's absolute braking distance to the end of authority (EoA at a TDS boundary). Speed profile options: each train may run with a choice of speed profiles (e.g., nominal, faster, slower/economical) affecting running times and braking distances. Distinguish switches from plain track resources (switches require route locking, plain sections only need section occupancy separation).

Requirements:
- Decision variables: entry/exit times of each train at each resource, ordering (precedence) binary variables on each resource, speed profile selection binaries per train, rerouting binaries per train per alternative route.
- Objective: minimize total (weighted) delay of all trains at their scheduled exit points (or at all timetable events).
- Constraints: 
  1. Running time constraints per resource depending on chosen speed profile.
  2. Minimum headway/separation constraints between consecutive trains on each resource, with headway depending on the speed profiles of the leading and following train (speed-dependent braking distance for DTG: separation = braking distance of follower at its speed + safety margin + length of TDS).
  3. Ordering constraints: if train i precedes train j on a resource, then exit_i <= entry_j; big-M disjunctions for the ordering binaries.
  4. Route consistency: if a train takes a route, it occupies exactly the resources of that route; rerouting binaries select one route per train.
  5. Switch constraints: mutual exclusion on switch resources with route locking (no two conflicting routes simultaneously).
  6. Timetable/delay constraints: actual times >= scheduled times (no early departure), delay variables = actual - scheduled, bounded.
  7. Rolling stock / dwell time constraints at stations.
- All constraints must be linear; use big-M for disjunctions. State assumptions explicitly (e.g., constant speeds per resource per profile, braking distances precomputed per (train, profile, resource) pair, given headway matrix h[i,j,resource,profile_i,profile_j])."}
function.name: or_operator

messages.content:
# MILP for Real-Time Railway Conflict Detection and Resolution under DTG Signalling (ETCS L2, TTD)

## 1. Assumptions

- The network is divided into fixed **TTD sections (TDS)**. Each resource r ∈ R is either a **plain TDS** or a **switch** (point zone).
- Each train i ∈ T has a scheduled route; a set of alternative routes Rᵢ (each a fixed ordered sequence of resources) is precomputed for rerouting.
- For each (train i, profile p) and each resource r on a route, the **running time** tᵢᵣₚ and **entry/exit speeds** are precomputed by simulation (constant average speed per resource per profile).
- **Braking distances** dᵦᵣₐₖₑ(i, p, r) to the EoA at the end of resource r are precomputed per (train, profile, resource).
- The **speed-dependent minimum headway** between trains i (leader, profile p) and j (follower, profile q) on resource r is precomputed:

  h[i,j,r,p,q] = dᵦᵣₐₖₑ(j, q, r) + s + L(TDS_r) + L(j) − dᵦᵣₐₖₑ(i, p, r)⁺

  (follower's braking distance + safety margin s + TDS length + follower train length, possibly reduced by leader's braking distance), all linear data.
- Switch resources require **route locking**: two conflicting switch routes cannot be active simultaneously (conflict set C given).
- Times are integer (minutes or seconds); big-M = M.

## 2. Sets and Parameters

| Symbol | Meaning |
|---|---|
| T | trains; R | track resources (TDS + switches) |
| Pᵢ | speed profiles of train i (nominal, faster, slower) |
| Rᵢ | alternative routes of train i; Rᵢᵣ = resources of route ρ |
| wᵢ | delay weight of train i |
| aᵢ, dᵢ | scheduled entry (origin departure) / exit (destination arrival) times |
| tᵢᵣₚ | running time of train i on r with profile p |
| dwᵢₛ | minimum dwell time of train i at station s |
| h[i,j,r,p,q] | speed-profile-dependent minimum headway |
| M | big-M constant |

## 3. Decision Variables

- eᵢᵣ, xᵢᵣ ∈ ℤ⁺ : entry / exit time of train i at resource r.
- yᵢⱼᵣ ∈ {0,1} : 1 if train i precedes train j on resource r (i before j).
- zᵢₚ ∈ {0,1} : 1 if train i uses speed profile p (∑ₚ zᵢₚ = 1).
- uᵢρ ∈ {0,1} : 1 if train i uses route ρ ∈ Rᵢ (∑ρ uᵢρ = 1).
- oᵢᵣ ∈ {0,1} : 1 if resource r is on the chosen route of train i (occupancy).
- Dᵢ ≥ 0 : delay of train i at its scheduled exit point.

## 4. Objective

Minimize total weighted delay:

**min ∑ᵢ wᵢ Dᵢ**

## 5. Constraints

**(1) Speed profile selection**

∑ₚ∈Pᵢ zᵢₚ = 1  ∀i ∈ T

**(2) Route consistency**

∑ρ∈Rᵢ uᵢρ = 1  ∀i ∈ T
oᵢᵣ = ∑ρ∈Rᵢ: r∈Rᵢρ uᵢρ  ∀i, ∀r ∈ R  (linear: r is occupied iff a chosen route contains it)

**(3) Running times (profile-dependent)**

xᵢᵣ − eᵢᵣ ≥ tᵢᵣᵐⁱⁿ − M(1 − zᵢₚ) − M(1 − oᵢᵣ)  ∀i, r, p
xᵢᵣ − eᵢᵣ ≤ tᵢᵣᵐᵃˣ + M(1 − zᵢₚ) + M(1 − oᵢᵣ)  ∀i, r, p

with tᵢᵣᵐⁱⁿ = tᵢᵣᵐᵃˣ = tᵢᵣₚ when profile p is fixed; if only one profile, drop z.

**(4) Ordering disjunctions (no-overlap on each resource, speed-dependent headways)**

For every pair i < j and every resource r, with profiles p (i) and q (j):

xᵢᵣ + h[i,j,r,p,q] − M(1 − yᵢⱼᵣ) ≤ eⱼᵣ + M(2 − zᵢₚ − zⱼq) + M(1 − oᵢᵣ) + M(1 − oⱼᵣ)
xⱼᵣ + h[j,i,r,q,p] − M·yᵢⱼᵣ ≤ eᵢᵣ + M(2 − zᵢₚ − zⱼq) + M(1 − oᵢᵣ) + M(1 − oⱼᵣ)

If both trains occupy r and i precedes j (yᵢⱼᵣ = 1), the first applies; otherwise the second. The headway h depends on both selected profiles (DTG braking-distance separation).

**(5) Route-flow (precedence along the chosen route)**

For consecutive resources r, r′ in route ρ of train i:

eᵢᵣ′ ≥ xᵢᵣ − M(1 − uᵢρ)

**(6) Switch constraints (route locking)**

For each switch resource r and each pair of conflicting movements (i, ρ) vs (j, σ), (i,ρ) ∈ C(j,σ), i ≠ j:

eⱼᵣ ≥ xᵢᵣ − M(3 − uᵢρ − uⱼσ − yᵢⱼᵣ)
eᵢᵣ ≥ xⱼᵣ − M(2 − uᵢρ − uⱼσ + yᵢⱼᵣ)

i.e., if both conflicting routes are selected, the ordering variable enforces mutual exclusion including route-locking release time (absorbed in h or added as a constant).

**(7) Timetable / delay constraints**

eᵢᵣₒᵣᵢᵍⁱⁿ ≥ dᵢ  ∀i (no early departure)
xᵢ,exit = ∑ρ uᵢρ · (scheduled exit via ρ) + Dᵢ  → linearized as:
xᵢ,exit ≥ aᵢ,ρ − M(1 − uᵢρ)  ∀ρ
Dᵢ ≥ xᵢ,exit − aᵢ,ρ − M(1 − uᵢρ)  ∀ρ
Dᵢ ≤ Dᵐᵃˣ

**(8) Dwell times at stations**

For station resources s with dwell requirement: xᵢₛ − eᵢₛ ≥ dwᵢₛ − M(1 − oᵢₛ)

**(9) Variable domains**

e, x, D ≥ 0 integer; y, z, u, o ∈ {0,1}.

## 6. Explanation of Model Elements

- **Retiming** is captured by e/x variables; **reordering** by the y binaries (big-M disjunctions, standard job-shop formulation); **rerouting** by u/o binaries selecting exactly one route per train.
- **DTG signalling** enters through the data h[i,j,r,p,q]: because the follower's EoA braking distance depends on its speed profile, separation is not a constant headway but a profile-pair-dependent parameter — the key enhancement over classical RECIFE-MILP.
- **Switches vs plain TDS**: plain resources need only constraint (4); switches additionally enforce route-locking mutual exclusion via (6).
- The model is a linear MILP (all nonlinearities precomputed into h and t parameters), solvable by branch-and-bound for real-time CR on regional networks.

If you'd like, I can instantiate this on a small example network with numeric data to show a concrete solution.

messages.content:
# MILP for Conflict Detection & Resolution (CDR) under DTG Signalling (ETCS L2)

## 1. Sets and Indices

| Symbol | Meaning |
|---|---|
| $I$ | set of trains, indexed $i, j$ |
| $R$ | set of track resources (block sections), indexed $r$ |
| $P_{ir}$ | set of running-time profiles of train $i$ on resource $r$ (e.g., speed profiles under different braking curves), indexed $p, q$ |
| $C$ | set of conflicting switch-route pairs $(r, s)$: occupying $r$ and $s$ simultaneously is not allowed (conflict graph edges) |
| $R_i \subseteq R$ | resources on the route of train $i$, in order; $r_{\text{prev}}(i,r)$ = predecessor of $r$ on $i$'s route |

## 2. Parameters

| Symbol | Meaning |
|---|---|
| $t_{irp}$ | running time of train $i$ on $r$ under profile $p$ |
| $h[i,j,r,p,q]$ | headway time between exit of $j$ and entry of $i$ on $r$ when $i$ uses profile $p$ and $j$ uses profile $q$ (asymmetric: $h[i,j,r,p,q] \neq h[j,i,r,q,p]$ in general) |
| $\ell_{rs}$ | route-locking release time for conflicting switch-route pair $(r,s)$ |
| $A_i$ | scheduled exit (arrival at destination) time of train $i$ |
| $e_i^{sched}$ | scheduled entry time of train $i$ at its origin resource |
| $\delta_i$ | initial delay of train $i$ (input) |
| $w_i \geq 0$ | delay weight of train $i$ |
| $M$ | sufficiently large constant |

## 3. Variables

| Symbol | Domain | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| $o_{ir}$ | binary | 1 if train $i$ occupies resource $r$ |
| $z_{ip}$ | binary | 1 if train $i$ selects profile $p$ (per resource: $z_{irp}$; written $z_{ip}$ per $(i,r)$ for brevity) |
| $y_{ijr}$ | binary, defined for $i<j$ | 1 if $i$ passes $r$ before $j$; $y_{jir} := 1 - y_{ijr}$ |
| $e_{ir}, x_{ir} \geq 0$ | continuous | entry / exit time of train $i$ on resource $r$ |
| $x_{i,\text{exit}} \geq 0$ | continuous | exit event of train $i$ (destination) |
| $D_i \geq 0$ | continuous | final delay of train $i$ |

## 4. Objective

$$\min \sum_{i \in I} w_i D_i \tag{OBJ}$$

## 5. Constraints

**(1) Route occupancy** — train $i$ occupies exactly the resources on its route:

$$o_{ir} = 1 \quad \forall i \in I,\ \forall r \in R_i \tag{1}$$

**(2) Profile selection** — exactly one running-time profile per occupied resource:

$$\sum_{p \in P_{ir}} z_{ip} = o_{ir} \quad \forall i \in I,\ \forall r \in R_i \tag{2}$$

**(3) Running time** (entry/exit consistency, active only when occupying $r$):

$$x_{ir} - e_{ir} \geq \sum_{p \in P_{ir}} t_{irp}\, z_{ip} - M(1 - o_{ir}) \quad \forall i, r \in R_i \tag{3a}$$

Optionally, if maximum running times apply:

$$x_{ir} - e_{ir} \leq \sum_{p \in P_{ir}} t_{irp}\, z_{ip} + s_{ir} + M(1 - o_{ir}) \quad \forall i, r \in R_i \tag{3b}$$

with slack variable $s_{ir} \geq 0$ (dwell/holding allowed on the resource).

**(4) Headway / ordering on each resource** — for each pair $i<j$, resource $r \in R_i \cap R_j$, and profile pair $(p,q)$, enforce exactly one of the two orderings; the constraint is active **only** when both trains occupy $r$ **and** the respective profiles are selected:

$$x_{ir} + h[i,j,r,p,q] \leq e_{jr} + M\,y_{ijr} + M(1-o_{ir}) + M(1-o_{jr}) + M(1-z_{ip}) + M(1-z_{jq}) \tag{4a}$$

$$x_{jr} + h[j,i,r,q,p] \leq e_{ir} + M(1-y_{ijr}) + M(1-o_{ir}) + M(1-o_{jr}) + M(1-z_{ip}) + M(1-z_{jq}) \tag{4b}$$

Since $y_{jir} = 1 - y_{ijr}$, exactly one of (4a)/(4b) is binding whenever both trains occupy $r$ with profiles $p$ and $q$ selected; otherwise the big-M terms relax it.

**(5) Route continuity** — consecutive resources on a route, active only when both are occupied:

$$e_{ir} \geq x_{i,r_{\text{prev}}(i,r)} - M(2 - o_{ir} - o_{i,r_{\text{prev}}(i,r)}) \quad \forall i,\ r \in R_i,\ r_{\text{prev}}(i,r) \neq \emptyset \tag{5}$$

Also $e_{ir}, x_{ir} \geq 0$ always; all timing constraints are relaxed by $o$ when the resource is not occupied.

**(6) Switch conflicts** — for each conflicting pair $(r,s) \in C$ and each pair of trains $i \neq j$ occupying them, mutual exclusion with route-locking release time $\ell_{rs}$; a single ordering binary $g_{ij}^{rs}$ (for $i<j$) decides which train is released first:

$$x_{ir} + \ell_{rs} \leq e_{js} + M\,g_{ij}^{rs} + M(1-o_{ir}) + M(1-o_{js}) \tag{6a}$$

$$x_{js} + \ell_{rs} \leq e_{ir} + M(1-g_{ij}^{rs}) + M(1-o_{js}) + M(1-o_{ir}) \tag{6b}$$

$$g_{ij}^{rs} \in \{0,1\} \tag{6c}$$

(Analogous constraints for the pair $(s,r)$ if both directions of the conflict graph are enumerated, or symmetrically with roles of $r,s$ swapped.)

**(7) Exit event and final delay** — single exit event per train, no early arrival:

$$x_{i,\text{exit}} \geq A_i \quad \forall i \in I \tag{7a}$$

$$D_i \geq x_{i,\text{exit}} - A_i \quad \forall i \in I \tag{7b}$$

$$D_i \geq 0 \tag{7c}$$

**(8) Initial conditions** — trains enter at their delayed actual entry time:

$$e_{i,\text{origin}(i)} = e_i^{sched} + \delta_i \quad \forall i \in I \tag{8}$$

## 6. Assumptions

1. **Routes are fixed inputs** ($R_i$ given); only timing and ordering are decided. Route choice would require additional binaries.
2. **DTG/ETCS L2 semantics**: each block section (resource) is exclusively occupied; headway $h$ depends on both trains' speed/braking profiles, hence the profile pair $(p,q)$ dependence.
3. **Profiles**: exactly one profile per (train, resource); profiles capture different deceleration/braking-curve behaviour, giving resource-dependent running and headway times.
4. **Switch conflicts** are precomputed as a conflict graph $C$; $\ell_{rs}$ models the route-locking release time before the conflicting route can be locked again.
5. **Big-M** must dominate any feasible time difference (e.g., $M \geq \max_i(A_i + \delta_i + \sum t) - \min_i e_i^{sched}$ plus all headways).
6. **Delays** are measured only at the destination exit event; early arrival is not allowed ($x_{i,\text{exit}} \geq A_i$), so $D_i$ correctly captures lateness.
7. **No overtaking within a resource** is implied by (4); overtaking across resources is possible if the $y$ orderings differ between consecutive resources.
8. All times are continuous (minutes or seconds); the model is a pure MILP with binaries $o, z, y, g$ and continuous $e, x, D, s$.

Route continuity (5) must then be conditioned on the chosen route: e_{ir} ≥ x_{i,r'} − M(1 − u_{iρ}) for consecutive r', r on route ρ. Keep everything else from the previous version (constraints 2–4, 6–8 unchanged in structure).

2. In (4), the headway h[i,j,r,p,q] should be defined explicitly for DTG: h = (braking distance of follower j under profile q to the EoA at end of r)/speed + safety margin + TDS length + train length j, minus any credit from leader i's braking distance — state this as precomputed data.

3. Add dwell-time constraints at station resources: x_{is} − e_{is} ≥ dw_{is} − M(1 − o_{is}).

4. Keep objective min Σ w_i D_i and all assumptions; produce the complete final model with numbered constraints."}
function.name: or_operator

messages.content:
# CDR MILP under DTG Signalling — Final Model

## Sets and indices
- $i, j \in T$: trains
- $r, r' \in R$: track resources (segments); $s \in S \subseteq R$: station resources
- $p, q \in P$: running profiles (speed profiles)
- $\rho \in \mathcal{R}_i$: candidate routes of train $i$
- $R_i \subseteq R$: resources usable by train $i$

## Precomputed data
- $br_{jq}$: braking distance of train $j$ under profile $q$ (m)
- $L_j$: length of train $j$ (m); $TDS_r$: train detection system length of resource $r$ (m)
- $m_{safety}$: safety margin (m); $v_{jq}$: speed of train $j$ under profile $q$ (m/s)
- **DTG headway (precomputed, per feedback item 2):**

$$h[i,j,r,p,q] = \frac{br_{jq}^{EoA(r)}}{v_{jq}} + m_{safety}/v_{jq} + TDS_r/v_{jq} + L_j/v_{jq} - \frac{br_{ip}^{EoA(r)}}{v_{ip}}$$

i.e. time for follower $j$ (profile $q$) to brake from its speed to the End of Authority at the end of $r$, plus safety margin, plus the TDS (track-section) length, plus train length $j$, **minus the credit** from leader $i$'s braking distance (leader braking closer to the EoA reduces required separation).
- $dw_{is}$: minimum dwell time of train $i$ at station $s$
- $M$: big-M; $w_i$: delay weight; $a_i$: ideal (unconstrained) exit time

## Variables
- $x_{ir} \ge 0$: entry (occupation start) time of train $i$ on resource $r$
- $e_{ir} \ge 0$: exit (release) time of train $i$ on resource $r$
- $o_{ir} \in \{0,1\}$: 1 if train $i$ occupies resource $r$
- $u_{i\rho} \in \{0,1\}$: 1 if train $i$ uses route $\rho \in \mathcal{R}_i$
- $D_i \ge 0$: delay of train $i$

## Model

**Objective (1):**
$$\min \sum_{i \in T} w_i D_i$$

**Route selection (2):**
$$\sum_{\rho \in \mathcal{R}_i} u_{i\rho} = 1 \qquad \forall i \in T$$

**Occupancy–route linking (3):**
$$o_{ir} = \sum_{\rho \in \mathcal{R}_i:\, r \in \rho} u_{i\rho} \qquad \forall i \in T,\ \forall r \in R_i$$

**Route continuity, conditioned on chosen route (4):**
$$e_{ir'} \le x_{ir}, \qquad e_{ir'} \ge x_{ir} - M(1 - u_{i\rho}) \qquad \forall i,\ \forall \rho \in \mathcal{R}_i,\ \forall (r', r) \text{ consecutive on } \rho$$

**Resource occupancy duration (5):**
$$e_{ir} \ge x_{ir} + \tau_{irp} - M(1 - o_{ir}) \qquad \forall i,\ r \in R_i,\ p \in P$$

**Dwell time at stations (6):**
$$x_{is} - e_{is} \ge dw_{is} - M(1 - o_{is}) \qquad \forall i \in T,\ \forall s \in S \cap R_i$$

**DTG headway / no-overlap (7):** for each ordered pair $(i,j)$, $i \ne j$, common resource $r$, profiles $p, q$:
$$x_{jr} \ge e_{ir} + h[i,j,r,p,q] - M(3 - o_{ir} - o_{jr} - y_{ijrp})$$
$$x_{ir} \ge e_{jr} + h[j,i,r,q,p] - M(4 - o_{ir} - o_{jr} - y_{ijrp})$$
$$y_{ijrp} \le o_{ir}, \quad y_{ijrp} \le o_{jr}, \quad y_{ijrp} \ge o_{ir} + o_{jr} - 1 \qquad \forall i<j,\ r,\ p$$
with $y_{ijrp} \in \{0,1\}$ indicating both trains occupy $r$ (ordering enforced in one direction only when both present).

**Delay definition (8):**
$$D_i \ge x_{i, r_i^{last}} - a_i, \qquad D_i \ge 0 \qquad \forall i \in T$$

**Variable domains (9):**
$$x_{ir}, e_{ir} \ge 0;\quad o_{ir}, u_{i\rho}, y_{ijrp} \in \{0,1\};\quad D_i \ge 0$$

## Explanation of elements
- **(2)–(3)** reintroduce local rerouting: each train picks exactly one route; occupancy variables are then determined by the route choice, so all resource-based constraints automatically apply only to resources on the chosen route.
- **(4)** enforces that consecutive resources on the *chosen* route are traversed in order (exit from $r'$ before/at entry to $r$); the big-M deactivates the constraint for routes not selected.
- **(5)** links running time $\tau_{irp}$ (profile-dependent) to occupancy; inactive if $r$ not occupied.
- **(6)** enforces minimum dwell at stations, active only when the station is on the chosen route.
- **(7)** implements DTG separation: the follower may enter $r$ only after the leader releases it plus the precomputed headway $h$, which accounts for braking-to-EoA time, safety margin, TDS length, follower train length, and subtracts the leader's braking-distance credit. The $y$ variables activate the constraint only when both trains occupy $r$.
- **(8)–(9)** define weighted delay relative to ideal times and complete the domain specification.

# CDR MILP under DTG Signalling (ETCS L2 with TTD) — Definitive Model

## 1. Sets and Indices

| Symbol | Meaning |
|---|---|
| $I$ | set of trains, indexed $i, j$ |
| $R$ | set of track resources (block sections / TTD sections), indexed $r, s$ |
| $P_i$ | set of running-time profiles (DTG speed profiles) available to train $i$, indexed $p, q$ |
| $\mathcal{R}_i$ | set of admissible routes for train $i$ through the network, indexed $\rho$; each route is an ordered sequence of resources |
| $C$ | set of conflicting switch-route pairs $(r,s)$: occupying $r$ locks $s$ until release |
| $E$ | set of consecutive resource pairs $(r, r')$ on routes (for continuity) |
| $i < j$ | fixed total ordering on train pairs used for ordering binaries |

## 2. Parameters

| Symbol | Meaning |
|---|---|
| $e_i^{sched}$ | scheduled departure time of train $i$ at its origin |
| $\delta_i$ | initial delay of train $i$ at origin (given) |
| $A_i$ | earliest allowed arrival time of train $i$ at its exit resource |
| $w_i$ | delay weight of train $i$ |
| $D_i^{dwell}(r)$ | minimum dwell time of train $i$ at station resource $r$ |
| $\tau_{irp}$ | pure running time of train $i$ over resource $r$ under profile $p$ |
| $br_{ip}^{EoA(r)}$ | braking distance of train $i$ under profile $p$ to End-of-Authority at resource $r$ |
| $v_{ip}$ | speed of train $i$ under profile $p$ |
| $m_{safety}$ | safety margin (time-equivalent) |
| $TDS_r$ | TTD section update delay at resource $r$ |
| $L_j$ | train length of train $j$ |
| $\ell_{rs}$ | route-locking release time for conflicting pair $(r,s)$ |
| $h[i,j,r,p,q]$ | DTG headway (see Constraint (7) definition below) |
| $M$ | sufficiently large big-M constant |
| $origin(i)$, $exit(i)$ | origin / exit resource of train $i$ |

**Headway definition (explicit, per item 5):**

$$h[i,j,r,p,q] \;=\; \frac{br_{jq}^{EoA(r)} + m_{safety} + TDS_r + L_j}{v_{jq}} \;-\; \frac{br_{ip}^{EoA(r)}}{v_{ip}}$$

This is the minimum time separation between train $i$ entering $r$ (profile $p$) and follower $j$ entering $r$ (profile $q$), accounting for the follower's braking distance to the EoA, the safety margin, the TTD update delay, and the leader's train length.

## 3. Variables

**Binary:**
- $z_{ip} \in \{0,1\}$: train $i$ uses running-time profile $p$.
- $u_{i\rho} \in \{0,1\}$: train $i$ is assigned route $\rho$.
- $o_{ir} \in \{0,1\}$: train $i$ occupies resource $r$.
- $y_{ijr} \in \{0,1\}$, for $i<j$ and $r \in R$: pure ordering variable — equals 1 if $i$ passes $r$ before $j$ (no occupancy semantics attached).
- $g_{ij}^{rs} \in \{0,1\}$, for $(r,s) \in C$, $i \neq j$: ordering of the two trains at the conflicting switch pair.

**Continuous (non-negative):**
- $x_{ir} \ge 0$: time train $i$ enters resource $r$.
- $e_{ir} \ge 0$: time train $i$ releases (exits) resource $r$.
- $D_i \ge 0$: total delay of train $i$ at its exit.

## 4. Objective

$$\min \; Z = \sum_{i \in I} w_i \, D_i$$

## 5. Constraints

**(1) Profile selection** — each train uses exactly one DTG profile:
$$\sum_{p \in P_i} z_{ip} = 1 \qquad \forall i \in I$$

**(2) Route selection** — each train uses exactly one route:
$$\sum_{\rho \in \mathcal{R}_i} u_{i\rho} = 1 \qquad \forall i \in I$$

**(3) Occupancy linking** — train $i$ occupies $r$ iff a chosen route contains $r$:
$$o_{ir} = \sum_{\rho \in \mathcal{R}_i:\, r \in \rho} u_{i\rho} \qquad \forall i \in I,\; r \in R$$

**(4) Route continuity** — if train $i$ takes route $\rho$, exit from a resource precedes entry into the next resource on that route:
$$e_{ir'} \le x_{ir} + M(1 - u_{i\rho}) \qquad \forall i \in I,\; \rho \in \mathcal{R}_i,\; (r,r') \text{ consecutive on } \rho$$

**(5) Initial conditions** — entry at origin equals scheduled time plus initial delay:
$$x_{i,\,origin(i)} = e_i^{sched} + \delta_i \qquad \forall i \in I$$

**(6) Running time** — release time follows entry plus the profile-dependent running time, active only when the train actually occupies the resource:
$$e_{ir} \ge x_{ir} + \sum_{p \in P_i} \tau_{irp}\, z_{ip} - M(1 - o_{ir}) \qquad \forall i \in I,\; r \in R$$

**(7) Headway (DTG-based)** — for every pair $i<j$, every common resource $r$, and every profile pair $(p,q) \in P_i \times P_j$:

If $i$ goes first ($y_{ijr}=1$):
$$x_{jr} \ge e_{ir} + h[i,j,r,p,q] - M(1 - y_{ijr}) - M(1 - o_{ir}) - M(1 - o_{jr}) - M(1 - z_{ip}) - M(1 - z_{jq})$$

If $j$ goes first ($y_{ijr}=0$):
$$x_{ir} \ge e_{jr} + h[j,i,r,q,p] - M\,y_{ijr} - M(1 - o_{ir}) - M(1 - o_{jr}) - M(1 - z_{ip}) - M(1 - z_{jq})$$

$\forall i<j,\; r \in R \text{ common to both routes},\; p \in P_i,\; q \in P_j$.

The constraint is relaxed unless both trains occupy $r$ (via $o_{ir}, o_{jr}$) and the corresponding profiles are selected ($z_{ip}, z_{jq}$); the ordering binary $y_{ijr}$ selects which of the two inequalities is enforced.

**(8) Switch conflict / route locking** — for each conflicting switch pair $(r,s) \in C$ and trains $i \neq j$:

$$x_{js} \ge e_{ir} + \ell_{rs} - M\, g_{ij}^{rs} - M(1 - o_{ir}) - M(1 - o_{js})$$
$$x_{is} \ge e_{jr} + \ell_{rs} - M(1 - g_{ij}^{rs}) - M(1 - o_{ir}) - M(1 - o_{js})$$

$\forall (r,s) \in C,\; \forall i \neq j \in I$. If both trains occupy the respective resources, $g_{ij}^{rs}$ decides which train passes first; the other must wait until the first releases $r$ plus the release time $\ell_{rs}$.

**(9) Dwell times** — minimum dwell at station resources:
$$e_{ir} \ge x_{ir} + D_i^{dwell}(r) - M(1 - o_{ir}) \qquad \forall i \in I,\; r \in R \text{ with } D_i^{dwell}(r) > 0$$

**(10) No early arrival at exit:**
$$x_{i,\,exit(i)} \ge A_i \qquad \forall i \in I$$

**(11) Delay definition:**
$$D_i \ge x_{i,\,exit(i)} - A_i \qquad \forall i \in I$$
$$D_i \ge 0 \qquad \forall i \in I$$

**(12) Variable domains:**
$$z_{ip},\, u_{i\rho},\, o_{ir},\, y_{ijr},\, g_{ij}^{rs} \in \{0,1\}; \qquad x_{ir},\, e_{ir},\, D_i \ge 0$$

## 6. Assumptions

1. **Fixed total order $i<j$** on trains is used only to index the ordering binaries $y_{ijr}$; both directions of passing are covered by the two inequalities in (7).
2. **$y_{ijr}$ is a pure ordering variable**: it carries no occupancy semantics; it is only relaxed/enforced through the big-M structure of (7). No additional linking constraint to $o_{ir}$ is needed.
3. **Big-M validity**: $M$ must exceed any feasible time span (e.g., $M = \max_i (e_i^{sched} + \delta_i) + \sum$ of all running/dwell times + all headways).
4. **Common resources**: headway constraints (7) are generated only for resources $r$ appearing in admissible routes of both trains; likewise (8) only for trains whose routes can contain the conflicting resources.
5. **DTG profiles** $\tau_{irp}$, $br_{ip}^{EoA(r)}$, $v_{ip}$ are precomputed offline from the DTG (speed/distance profile) under ETCS L2 with TTD; the headway $h[i,j,r,p,q]$ is a parameter, not a variable.
6. **TTD granularity**: resources $r$ are TTD sections; $TDS_r$ captures the position-report/update delay of the train detection system.
7. **Route locking**: a route through switch resource $r$ locks conflicting resource $s$ until the train releases $r$ plus $\ell_{rs}$ (Constraint (8)).
8. **Delay** is measured at the exit resource against the earliest allowed arrival $A_i$; since the objective minimizes weighted $D_i$, Constraint (11) makes $D_i = \max(0, x_{i,exit} - A_i)$ at optimum.
9. **Single-threaded passage**: each train enters each resource on its route exactly once (no re-entry), consistent with the route sequences in $\mathcal{R}_i$.

# CDR MILP under DTG Signalling — Final Model

## Sets and indices
- $i, j \in T$: trains
- $r, r' \in R$: track resources (segments); $s \in S \subseteq R$: station resources
- $p, q \in P$: running profiles (speed profiles)
- $\rho \in \mathcal{R}_i$: candidate routes of train $i$
- $R_i \subseteq R$: resources usable by train $i$

## Precomputed data
- $br_{jq}$: braking distance of train $j$ under profile $q$ (m)
- $L_j$: length of train $j$ (m); $TDS_r$: train detection system length of resource $r$ (m)
- $m_{safety}$: safety margin (m); $v_{jq}$: speed of train $j$ under profile $q$ (m/s)
- **DTG headway (precomputed, per feedback item 2):**

$$h[i,j,r,p,q] = \frac{br_{jq}^{EoA(r)}}{v_{jq}} + m_{safety}/v_{jq} + TDS_r/v_{jq} + L_j/v_{jq} - \frac{br_{ip}^{EoA(r)}}{v_{ip}}$$

i.e. time for follower $j$ (profile $q$) to brake from its speed to the End of Authority at the end of $r$, plus safety margin, plus the TDS (track-section) length, plus train length $j$, **minus the credit** from leader $i$'s braking distance (leader braking closer to the EoA reduces required separation).
- $dw_{is}$: minimum dwell time of train $i$ at station $s$
- $M$: big-M; $w_i$: delay weight; $a_i$: ideal (unconstrained) exit time

## Variables
- $x_{ir} \ge 0$: entry (occupation start) time of train $i$ on resource $r$
- $e_{ir} \ge 0$: exit (release) time of train $i$ on resource $r$
- $o_{ir} \in \{0,1\}$: 1 if train $i$ occupies resource $r$
- $u_{i\rho} \in \{0,1\}$: 1 if train $i$ uses route $\rho \in \mathcal{R}_i$
- $D_i \ge 0$: delay of train $i$

## Model

**Objective (1):**
$$\min \sum_{i \in T} w_i D_i$$

**Route selection (2):**
$$\sum_{\rho \in \mathcal{R}_i} u_{i\rho} = 1 \qquad \forall i \in T$$

**Occupancy–route linking (3):**
$$o_{ir} = \sum_{\rho \in \mathcal{R}_i:\, r \in \rho} u_{i\rho} \qquad \forall i \in T,\ \forall r \in R_i$$

**Route continuity, conditioned on chosen route (4):**
$$e_{ir'} \le x_{ir}, \qquad e_{ir'} \ge x_{ir} - M(1 - u_{i\rho}) \qquad \forall i,\ \forall \rho \in \mathcal{R}_i,\ \forall (r', r) \text{ consecutive on } \rho$$

**Resource occupancy duration (5):**
$$e_{ir} \ge x_{ir} + \tau_{irp} - M(1 - o_{ir}) \qquad \forall i,\ r \in R_i,\ p \in P$$

**Dwell time at stations (6):**
$$x_{is} - e_{is} \ge dw_{is} - M(1 - o_{is}) \qquad \forall i \in T,\ \forall s \in S \cap R_i$$

**DTG headway / no-overlap (7):** for each ordered pair $(i,j)$, $i \ne j$, common resource $r$, profiles $p, q$:
$$x_{jr} \ge e_{ir} + h[i,j,r,p,q] - M(3 - o_{ir} - o_{jr} - y_{ijrp})$$
$$x_{ir} \ge e_{jr} + h[j,i,r,q,p] - M(4 - o_{ir} - o_{jr} - y_{ijrp})$$
$$y_{ijrp} \le o_{ir}, \quad y_{ijrp} \le o_{jr}, \quad y_{ijrp} \ge o_{ir} + o_{jr} - 1 \qquad \forall i<j,\ r,\ p$$
with $y_{ijrp} \in \{0,1\}$ indicating both trains occupy $r$ (ordering enforced in one direction only when both present).

**Delay definition (8):**
$$D_i \ge x_{i, r_i^{last}} - a_i, \qquad D_i \ge 0 \qquad \forall i \in T$$

**Variable domains (9):**
$$x_{ir}, e_{ir} \ge 0;\quad o_{ir}, u_{i\rho}, y_{ijrp} \in \{0,1\};\quad D_i \ge 0$$

## Explanation of elements
- **(2)–(3)** reintroduce local rerouting: each train picks exactly one route; occupancy variables are then determined by the route choice, so all resource-based constraints automatically apply only to resources on the chosen route.
- **(4)** enforces that consecutive resources on the *chosen* route are traversed in order (exit from $r'$ before/at entry to $r$); the big-M deactivates the constraint for routes not selected.
- **(5)** links running time $\tau_{irp}$ (profile-dependent) to occupancy; inactive if $r$ not occupied.
- **(6)** enforces minimum dwell at stations, active only when the station is on the chosen route.
- **(7)** implements DTG separation: the follower may enter $r$ only after the leader releases it plus the precomputed headway $h$, which accounts for braking-to-EoA time, safety margin, TDS length, follower train length, and subtracts the leader's braking-distance credit. The $y$ variables activate the constraint only when both trains occupy $r$.
- **(8)–(9)** define weighted delay relative to ideal times and complete the domain specification.
